assistantMessageEvent.content:
Checking McClatchy's yes and Mercury News' no reasoning more carefully. Also looking for full editorials from the Sacramento Bee or LA Times.

Enough information gathered. The vote removes a legal ban and sets minimum conditions without spending money on campaigns. Future programs would require separate political decisions.

The strongest argument against the measure is that it creates an incomplete permission structure. It allows officials to create programs by ordinance without another public vote. It lacks independent enforcement and meaningful caps on subsidies. Public money could stack on special-interest money. Several editorial boards that agree with the underlying concern still oppose it.

The strongest argument for yes is that the ban itself is the binding constraint blocking good programs. Charter cities already experiment with these laws, but the ban arbitrarily prevents everyone else from doing so. Specific statewide programs failed at the ballot because they included tax increases and one-size-fits-all designs. An opt-in enabling law is the correct institutional response to that history.

The measure includes stronger guardrails than opponents claim. It bans loan repayments and legal defense spending. It sets a $10 small-dollar limit. It protects against earmarks. It mandates spending limits and nondiscrimination.

Voluntary public financing is one of the few constitutional tools left in a post-Citizens United world.

The League of Women Voters, Common Cause, and Clean Money Campaign support it. McClatchy and the LA Times Skelton also say yes.

A no vote preserves a system where only personal wealth and large donors fund campaigns. That is worse than the risk of some poorly designed local programs.

The recommendation is yes. A failed vote would leave the statewide ban intact, and poorly designed programs could not be repealed locally. Charter cities are already exempt from that ban.

About 125 of California's 482 cities are charter cities. Most local governments are general law and remain banned. Counties are also prohibited from using public funds for campaigns.

The LAO and AG summaries disagree on whether charter counties are exempt from the ban. The LAO cites only certain charter cities, while the AG summary includes counties. The Johnson v. Bradley ruling applies home rule protections to charter cities but not to counties.

If only charter cities are exempt, counties would remain banned. County offices and state offices receive heavy special interest funding. This is a major concern. I will verify whether charter counties are also exempt.

I am also checking whether the measure's trigger mechanism is constitutional. I will verify whether its flaws are fatal enough to warrant a rejection. My leaning remains yes. The expected value of passing is moderate: several cities and possibly the state would experiment with well-designed small-donor match programs.

Clean Money and Common Cause would push for sound designs, and existing programs would serve as models. Some cities might still create weak or captured programs. Nondiscrimination rules and spending limits would constrain the worst abuses. Bad programs could be defunded by future budgets because they are not constitutional entitlements.

The measure does not appropriate a fixed sum. A bad program is reversible by the same body that created it, or by voters via referendum or initiative.

Passing would let more non-wealthy candidates run, strengthen small-donor power, and allow voluntary spending limits that are otherwise unconstitutional to impose. It would also reduce dependence on large donors in participating races.

A no vote preserves the status quo where billionaire self-funders and independent expenditure committees dominate. Qualified non-wealthy candidates stay out of races. Charter cities keep their programs, but everyone else remains blocked from experimentation.

The "wait for a better measure" strategy has failed for 38 years. A no vote is not a vote for reform; it is a vote to preserve the ban. The measure locks in permission rather than spending, so wasteful programs can be ended without another statewide constitutional fight.

The option value of lifting the ban outweighs keeping it. Bad programs can be ended locally, while good ones are currently impossible outside charter cities.

The Chronicle's call to study first is weak. Existing charter city programs have been available for decades without study. Waiting for a study that nobody is commissioning is a reason to delay forever. Studying those programs does not require maintaining the ban on new ones.

The blank check argument is overstated. A yes vote only authorizes future appropriations that would still go through normal budget processes, and existing local programs are modest. The lack of independent enforcement remains the strongest anti-argument, but it is not decisive.

The PRA's disclosure rules still apply to public campaign funds. The FPPC retains enforcement authority over contribution limits and prohibitions in 85300(a)-(d) and (g)-(h). It only excuses itself from administering local public financing systems. A candidate who uses public funds for legal defense would violate the PRA. Local prosecutors, civil litigants, and local ethics bodies can enforce that prohibition.

Opposition claims that the measure lacks spending limits, strict criteria, or that it would drain school and public safety funds are incorrect. The text explicitly requires expenditure limits and defines the $10 small-donor threshold. Earmarked funds are prohibited, and any general fund tradeoffs would be a local choice rather than a mandate.

Opposition claims that thousands of candidates will automatically receive money are incorrect; the measure only authorizes future programs and requires local qualification. The argument that it allows special interest money is misleading because the current system already permits such funding, and matching systems are designed to work alongside limited private contributions.

Supporter overclaims should be rejected. The claim that elections will be "won not bought" is overstated because independent expenditure committees and self-funding remain possible. The "$1 per resident" figure is marketing hyperbole rather than a binding cap.

The URL points to the 2026 public financing measure, not a 2024 climate bond. The recommendation remains yes.

I considered a steelman argument for no: public financing only works if private money is replaced by tightly capped public funds with strong enforcement, and Prop 4 does not lock that in. I rejected it. The recommendation remains yes.

The measure authorizes additive public subsidies with caps and qualification rules written by beneficiaries, enforced by nobody in particular. Empirical evidence shows that poorly designed programs do not reduce donor influence. California's track record of interest-group capture makes this especially risky. The Legislature had the opportunity to propose a specific, capped, independently administered program, but chose a blank permission structure instead because voters reject specific programs.

The measure is not a true laboratory of democracy. It avoids voter accountability for program costs. Voters have rejected similar proposals three times. The foreign-money penalty is a Trojan sweetener. Former FPPC chairs oppose the measure. Multiple editorial boards, including the Chronicle, also oppose it.

The no vote is fiscally responsible and institutionally careful. A better measure would require independent administration, minimum small-donor thresholds, capped public subsidies, and mandatory rejection of large contributions. The choice is between Prop 4 and the ban, not between this measure and a hypothetical ideal.

The ideal program is not on the ballot and is unlikely to appear, given prior rejections. A no vote would kill reform by demanding perfection. The measure is a floor, not a ceiling. Implementing statutes and ordinances can add strong safeguards after passage. Cities can still adopt well-designed local systems.

The Chronicle's call for both maximum local freedom and mandated best practices is internally inconsistent. Lange's approach of maximum freedom is consistent with the measure's theory.

The risk that jurisdictions will choose bad designs is mitigated by annual budget visibility, reversibility, and existing models to copy.

The recommendation remains yes.

The SF Chronicle, the most sophisticated local policy voice, voted no. That carries significant weight.

The blank check argument is overstated. A yes vote only authorizes future appropriations that would still go through normal budget processes, and existing local programs are modest. The lack of independent enforcement remains the strongest anti-argument, but it is not decisive.

The PRA's disclosure rules still apply to public campaign funds. The FPPC retains enforcement authority over contribution limits and prohibitions in 85300(a)-(d) and (g)-(h). It only excuses itself from administering local public financing systems. A candidate who uses public funds for legal defense would violate the PRA. Local prosecutors, civil litigants, and local ethics bodies can enforce that prohibition.

Opposition claims that the measure lacks spending limits, strict criteria, or that it would drain school and public safety funds are incorrect. The text explicitly requires expenditure limits and defines the $10 small-donor threshold. Earmarked funds are prohibited, and any general fund tradeoffs would be a local choice rather than a mandate.

Opposition claims that thousands of candidates will automatically receive money are incorrect; the measure only authorizes future programs and requires local qualification. The argument that it allows special interest money is misleading because the current system already permits such funding, and matching systems are designed to work alongside limited private contributions.

Supporter overclaims should be rejected. The claim that elections will be "won not bought" is overstated because independent expenditure committees and self-funding remain possible. The "$1 per resident" figure is marketing hyperbole rather than a binding cap.

The URL points to the 2026 public financing measure, not a 2024 climate bond. The recommendation remains yes.

I considered a steelman argument for no: public financing only works if private money is replaced by tightly capped public funds with strong enforcement, and Prop 4 does not lock that in. I rejected it. The recommendation remains yes.

The measure authorizes additive public subsidies with caps and qualification rules written by beneficiaries, enforced by nobody in particular. Empirical evidence shows that poorly designed programs do not reduce donor influence. California's track record of interest-group capture makes this especially risky. The Legislature had the opportunity to propose a specific, capped, independently administered program, but chose a blank permission structure instead because voters reject specific programs.

The measure is not a true laboratory of democracy. It avoids voter accountability for program costs. Voters have rejected similar proposals three times. The foreign-money penalty is a Trojan sweetener. Former FPPC chairs oppose the measure. Multiple editorial boards, including the Chronicle, also oppose it.

The no vote is fiscally responsible and institutionally careful. A better measure would require independent administration, minimum small-donor thresholds, capped public subsidies, and mandatory rejection of large contributions. The choice is between Prop 4 and the ban, not between this measure and a hypothetical ideal.

The ideal program is not on the ballot and is unlikely to appear, given prior rejections. A no vote would kill reform by demanding perfection. The measure is a floor, not a ceiling. Implementing statutes and ordinances can add strong safeguards after passage. Cities can still adopt well-designed local systems.

The Chronicle's call for both maximum local freedom and mandated best practices is internally inconsistent. Lange's approach of maximum freedom is consistent with the measure's theory.

The risk that jurisdictions will choose bad designs is mitigated by annual budget visibility, reversibility, and existing models to copy.

The recommendation remains yes.

The SF Chronicle, the most sophisticated local policy voice, voted no. That carries significant weight.

The influence of money on political races has gotten out of control, but allowing candidates to accept public funds — taxpayer dollars — for campaign purposes is not the answer.
We recommend voting “no” on Proposition 4. Our tax dollars should not be spent on election campaigns.

Endorsement: Reject San Mateo Community College District’s $848 million Measure V (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-reject-san-mateo-community-college-districts-848-million-measure-v/)
Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
Sky-high spending
Consider this news organization’s report last week (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/11/whos-donating-to-the-billionaire-backed-group-has-raised-almost-300-million-to-fight-the-wealth-tax/) showing how a single political action committee backed by billionaires — Building a Better California — has spent nearly a quarter of a billion dollars this year alone, breaking all previous records.
Understandably alarmed, this inundation of money into state politics has pushed legislators to ask voters this November to repeal a 1988 law and allow taxpayer dollars to be spent on campaigns.
A “yes” vote would allow state and local governments to create programs so that public funds — again, taxpayer dollars — could be set aside for election campaigns.
We understand the desire to take corporate money out of elections.
This year’s race for California governor (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/california-governor-contributions-takeaways/) highlights that need more than ever. A political spending committee comprising the state realtors association, California Chamber of Commerce, Pacific Gas & Electric and the state electrical workers union spent a record $32 million on ads opposing Democratic billionaire Tom Steyer, who ultimately placed third in the primary.
Leading into those primaries, Democratic nominee Xavier Becerra — whose name appears on the Nov. 3 ballot — was backed by Meta, AirBnB and Uber at $1 million each and Chevron, McDonalds and DaVita at $500,000 each, to name a few.
Those corporate dollars force the fair question: If elected, how confident are we that Becerra will have the people’s interests at heart, and not those corporations’?
Not solution
Many counties are already struggling financially. Some have placed sales tax measures on the ballot this year to bring more revenue into their general funds. Some already had sales tax measures on the ballot in 2024. And some still face a budget deficit. Other counties may be sitting on the fence, but there is no wiggle room in their budgets to create a fund for campaign financing.
Moreover, people should be able to decide if they want their money to go toward supporting a candidate. Our elected officials should not make that decision for us — especially if they are up for re-election.
We agree that special interests should not be able to buy candidates or campaigns, but Proposition 4 is not the answer. Creating a fund of taxpayer dollars and making it available for election campaigns is not the answer. Those hard-earned dollars belong in a municipality’s general fund, to be used on improving roadways, funding for public safety officers or enhancing our local parks.
Reject Proposition 4.

McClatchy Media’s endorsements for all 14 propositions on California’s ballot
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
Updated October 27, 2026 9:16 AM
The California state Capitol on Aug. 31, 2026.
Lauren Chapman
lchapman@sacbee.com
Opinion journalists for McClatchy Media conducted interviews with supporters and opponents of all 14 statewide propositions on your November ballot. The journalists then deliberated and decided how they would vote on each one, just as voters do. Their endorsements, linked below, explain their positions.
What to Know
Here are key takeaways:
Prop. 1 would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds for affordable housing and CalVet home loans (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317326136.html#storylink=var-wtk), with $10 billion aimed at closing financing gaps for nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes already in the pipeline. The board endorsed a “yes” vote but urged the state to publish a transparent dashboard tracking costs and results.
Prop. 2 would raise California’s rainy day fund cap from 10% to 20% (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317091637.html#storylink=var-wtk) of annual tax collections and allow some reserves to pay down state debts, including $20 billion still owed to the federal government for pandemic-era unemployment borrowing. The board recommended a “yes” vote as a safeguard against future downturns.
Prop. 3 would make permanent a tax on California’s top 2% of earners (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317445836.html#storylink=var-wtk) — single filers making at least $361,000 and joint filers at least $721,000 — that generates between $5 billion and $15 billion a year for schools and community colleges. The board endorsed a “yes” vote.
Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on public financing of state and local campaigns (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317448027.html#storylink=var-wtk), allowing matching-fund or public-grant programs for qualifying candidates. The board backed a “yes” vote, arguing public financing reduces reliance on wealthy donors.
Prop. 5 would eliminate the second question on recall ballots asking who should replace an ousted official (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316911387.html#storylink=var-wtk), instead triggering special elections or gubernatorial appointments. The board strongly endorsed a “yes” vote, noting past recalls have installed replacements with less voter support than the official removed.
Prop. 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to finance second mortgages (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317470188.html#storylink=var-wtk) covering up to 17% of a new home’s price for middle-class buyers. Despite reservations about default risk, the board recommended a “yes” vote.
Prop. 38 proposes an $8.4 billion bond for immunology research (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166634.html#storylink=var-wtk), with half guaranteed to an institute tied to UCLA and backed by billionaire physician Gary K. Michelson. The board urged a “no” vote, warning the measure would exempt the institute from public-records laws.
Prop. 39 would require government-issued ID at the polls and partial ID numbers on mail ballots (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317017898.html#storylink=var-wtk), with backers including nine billionaires tracked by Forbes. The board recommended a “no” vote, warning the measure would disenfranchise more legitimate voters than it would stop fraudulent ones.
Prop. 40 would impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on Californians worth more than $1 billion (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317269166.html#storylink=var-wtk), with 90% of proceeds reserved for healthcare amid federal Medi-Cal cuts projected to cost 1.3 million residents coverage by 2030. A majority of the board endorsed a “yes” vote.
Prop. 41 is a constitutional amendment backed by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other wealthy donors that would ban taxes exempt from state spending limits on or after Jan. 1, 2026 (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html#storylink=var-wtk) — a provision that could nullify Prop. 40. The board urged a “no” vote.
Prop. 42 is billed as a safeguard for 401(k) accounts and personal property, but the board called it a “poison pill” designed to derail the billionaire wealth tax (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166989.html#storylink=var-wtk) in Prop. 40. If Prop. 42 gets more yes votes than Prop. 40, Prop. 40 would not take effect. Vote “no,” the board said.
Prop. 43 would raise the threshold to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives from a simple majority to 66.7% (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316956235.html#storylink=var-wtk), giving a 33.3% minority the power to block measures funding fire, police, flood control and other local services. The board opposed it and urged a “no” vote.
Prop. 44, the Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act, would require federally qualified health centers to spend at least 90% of revenue on patient services (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317472706.html#storylink=var-wtk), up from the roughly 80% most currently report. The board recommended a “no” vote, citing warnings the mandate could force clinics serving nearly 7 million patients to close.
Prop. 45 would reshape the California Environmental Quality Act (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317475362.html#storylink=var-wtk) by tightening deadlines, limiting public-comment periods and barring judges from halting entire projects over partial violations. The board endorsed a “yes” vote, arguing CEQA has too often been used to block needed housing.
The summary points above were compiled with the help of AI tools and edited by journalists. The source reporting referenced above was written and edited entirely by journalists.

The influence of money on political races has gotten out of control, but allowing candidates to accept public funds — taxpayer dollars — for campaign purposes is not the answer.
We recommend voting “no” on Proposition 4. Our tax dollars should not be spent on election campaigns.

Sky-high spending
Consider this news organization’s report last week (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/11/whos-donating-to-the-billionaire-backed-group-has-raised-almost-300-million-to-fight-the-wealth-tax/) showing how a single political action committee backed by billionaires — Building a Better California — has spent nearly a quarter of a billion dollars this year alone, breaking all previous records.
Understandably alarmed, this inundation of money into state politics has pushed legislators to ask voters this November to repeal a 1988 law and allow taxpayer dollars to be spent on campaigns.
A “yes” vote would allow state and local governments to create programs so that public funds — again, taxpayer dollars — could be set aside for election campaigns.
We understand the desire to take corporate money out of elections.
This year’s race for California governor (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/california-governor-contributions-takeaways/) highlights that need more than ever. A political spending committee comprising the state realtors association, California Chamber of Commerce, Pacific Gas & Electric and the state electrical workers union spent a record $32 million on ads opposing Democratic billionaire Tom Steyer, who ultimately placed third in the primary.
Leading into those primaries, Democratic nominee Xavier Becerra — whose name appears on the Nov. 3 ballot — was backed by Meta, AirBnB and Uber at $1 million each and Chevron, McDonalds and DaVita at $500,000 each, to name a few.
Those corporate dollars force the fair question: If elected, how confident are we that Becerra will have the people’s interests at heart, and not those corporations’?
Not solution
Many counties are already struggling financially. Some have placed sales tax measures on the ballot this year to bring more revenue into their general funds. Some already had sales tax measures on the ballot in 2024. And some still face a budget deficit. Other counties may be sitting on the fence, but there is no wiggle room in their budgets to create a fund for campaign financing.
Moreover, people should be able to decide if they want their money to go toward supporting a candidate. Our elected officials should not make that decision for us — especially if they are up for re-election.
We agree that special interests should not be able to buy candidates or campaigns, but Proposition 4 is not the answer. Creating a fund of taxpayer dollars and making it available for election campaigns is not the answer. Those hard-earned dollars belong in a municipality’s general fund, to be used on improving roadways, funding for public safety officers or enhancing our local parks.
Reject Proposition 4.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: October 19, 2026 at 3:30 PM PDT | UPDATED: October 20, 2026 at 11:11 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
The influence of money on political races has gotten out of control, but allowing candidates to accept public funds — taxpayer dollars — for campaign purposes is not the answer.
We recommend voting “no” on Proposition 4. Our tax dollars should not be spent on election campaigns.

Sky-high spending
Consider this news organization’s report last week (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/11/whos-donating-to-the-billionaire-backed-group-has-raised-almost-300-million-to-fight-the-wealth-tax/) showing how a single political action committee backed by billionaires — Building a Better California — has spent nearly a quarter of a billion dollars this year alone, breaking all previous records.
Understandably alarmed, this inundation of money into state politics has pushed legislators to ask voters this November to repeal a 1988 law and allow taxpayer dollars to be spent on campaigns.
A “yes” vote would allow state and local governments to create programs so that public funds — again, taxpayer dollars — could be set aside for election campaigns.
We understand the desire to take corporate money out of elections.
This year’s race for California governor (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/california-governor-contributions-takeaways/) highlights that need more than ever. A political spending committee comprising the state realtors association, California Chamber of Commerce, Pacific Gas & Electric and the state electrical workers union spent a record $32 million on ads opposing Democratic billionaire Tom Steyer, who ultimately placed third in the primary.
Leading into those primaries, Democratic nominee Xavier Becerra — whose name appears on the Nov. 3 ballot — was backed by Meta, AirBnB and Uber at $1 million each and Chevron, McDonalds and DaVita at $500,000 each, to name a few.
Those corporate dollars force the fair question: If elected, how confident are we that Becerra will have the people’s interests at heart, and not those corporations’?
Not solution
Many counties are already struggling financially. Some have placed sales tax measures on the ballot this year to bring more revenue into their general funds. Some already had sales tax measures on the ballot in 2024. And some still face a budget deficit. Other counties may be sitting on the fence, but there is no wiggle room in their budgets to create a fund for campaign financing.
Moreover, people should be able to decide if they want their money to go toward supporting a candidate. Our elected officials should not make that decision for us — especially if they are up for re-election.
We agree that special interests should not be able to buy candidates or campaigns, but Proposition 4 is not the answer. Creating a fund of taxpayer dollars and making it available for election campaigns is not the answer. Those hard-earned dollars belong in a municipality’s general fund, to be used on improving roadways, funding for public safety officers or enhancing our local parks.
Reject Proposition 4.

McClatchy Media’s endorsements for all 14 propositions on California’s ballot
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
Updated October 27, 2026 9:16 AM
The California state Capitol on Aug. 31, 2026.
Lauren Chapman
lchapman@sacbee.com
Opinion journalists for McClatchy Media conducted interviews with supporters and opponents of all 14 statewide propositions on your November ballot. The journalists then deliberated and decided how they would vote on each one, just as voters do. Their endorsements, linked below, explain their positions.
What to Know
Here are key takeaways:
Prop. 1 would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds for affordable housing and CalVet home loans (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317326136.html#storylink=var-wtk), with $10 billion aimed at closing financing gaps for nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes already in the pipeline. The board endorsed a “yes” vote but urged the state to publish a transparent dashboard tracking costs and results.
Prop. 2 would raise California’s rainy day fund cap from 10% to 20% (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317091637.html#storylink=var-wtk) of annual tax collections and allow some reserves to pay down state debts, including $20 billion still owed to the federal government for pandemic-era unemployment borrowing. The board recommended a “yes” vote as a safeguard against future downturns.
Prop. 3 would make permanent a tax on California’s top 2% of earners (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317445836.html#storylink=var-wtk) — single filers making at least $361,000 and joint filers at least $721,000 — that generates between $5 billion and $15 billion a year for schools and community colleges. The board endorsed a “yes” vote.
Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on public financing of state and local campaigns (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317448027.html#storylink=var-wtk), allowing matching-fund or public-grant programs for qualifying candidates. The board backed a “yes” vote, arguing public financing reduces reliance on wealthy donors.
Prop. 5 would eliminate the second question on recall ballots asking who should replace an ousted official (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316911387.html#storylink=var-wtk), instead triggering special elections or gubernatorial appointments. The board strongly endorsed a “yes” vote, noting past recalls have installed replacements with less voter support than the official removed.
Prop. 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to finance second mortgages (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317470188.html#storylink=var-wtk) covering up to 17% of a new home’s price for middle-class buyers. Despite reservations about default risk, the board recommended a “yes” vote.
Prop. 38 proposes an $8.4 billion bond for immunology research (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166634.html#storylink=var-wtk), with half guaranteed to an institute tied to UCLA and backed by billionaire physician Gary K. Michelson. The board urged a “no” vote, warning the measure would exempt the institute from public-records laws.
Prop. 39 would require government-issued ID at the polls and partial ID numbers on mail ballots (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317017898.html#storylink=var-wtk), with backers including nine billionaires tracked by Forbes. The board recommended a “no” vote, warning the measure would disenfranchise more legitimate voters than it would stop fraudulent ones.
Prop. 40 would impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on Californians worth more than $1 billion (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317269166.html#storylink=var-wtk), with 90% of proceeds reserved for healthcare amid federal Medi-Cal cuts projected to cost 1.3 million residents coverage by 2030. A majority of the board endorsed a “yes” vote.
Prop. 41 is a constitutional amendment backed by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other wealthy donors that would ban taxes exempt from state spending limits on or after Jan. 1, 2026 (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html#storylink=var-wtk) — a provision that could nullify Prop. 40. The board urged a “no” vote.
Prop. 42 is billed as a safeguard for 401(k) accounts and personal property, but the board called it a “poison pill” designed to derail the billionaire wealth tax (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166989.html#storylink=var-wtk) in Prop. 40. If Prop. 42 gets more yes votes than Prop. 40, Prop. 40 would not take effect. Vote “no,” the board said.
Prop. 43 would raise the threshold to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives from a simple majority to 66.7% (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316956235.html#storylink=var-wtk), giving a 33.3% minority the power to block measures funding fire, police, flood control and other local services. The board opposed it and urged a “no” vote.
Prop. 44, the Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act, would require federally qualified health centers to spend at least 90% of revenue on patient services (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317472706.html#storylink=var-wtk), up from the roughly 80% most currently report. The board recommended a “no” vote, citing warnings the mandate could force clinics serving nearly 7 million patients to close.
Prop. 45 would reshape the California Environmental Quality Act (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317475362.html#storylink=var-wtk) by tightening deadlines, limiting public-comment periods and barring judges from halting entire projects over partial violations. The board endorsed a “yes” vote, arguing CEQA has too often been used to block needed housing.
The summary points above were compiled with the help of AI tools and edited by journalists. The source reporting referenced above was written and edited entirely by journalists.

Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on public financing of state and local campaigns (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317448027.html#storylink=var-wtk), allowing matching-fund or public-grant programs for qualifying candidates. The board backed a “yes” vote, arguing public financing reduces reliance on wealthy donors.
Prop. 5 would eliminate the second question on recall ballots asking who should replace an ousted official (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316911387.html#storylink=var-wtk), instead triggering special elections or gubernatorial appointments. The board strongly endorsed a “yes” vote, noting past recalls have installed replacements with less voter support than the official removed.
Prop. 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to finance second mortgages (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317470188.html#storylink=var-wtk) covering up to 17% of a new home’s price for middle-class buyers. Despite reservations about default risk, the board recommended a “yes” vote.
Prop. 38 proposes an $8.4 billion bond for immunology research (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166634.html#storylink=var-wtk), with half guaranteed to an institute tied to UCLA and backed by billionaire physician Gary K. Michelson. The board urged a “no” vote, warning the measure would exempt the institute from public-records laws.
Prop. 39 would require government-issued ID at the polls and partial ID numbers on mail ballots (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317017898.html#storylink=var-wtk), with backers including nine billionaires tracked by Forbes. The board recommended a “no” vote, warning the measure would disenfranchise more legitimate voters than it would stop fraudulent ones.
Prop. 40 would impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on Californians worth more than $1 billion (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317269166.html#storylink=var-wtk), with 90% of proceeds reserved for healthcare amid federal Medi-Cal cuts projected to cost 1.3 million residents coverage by 2030. A majority of the board endorsed a “yes” vote.
Prop. 41 is a constitutional amendment backed by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other wealthy donors that would ban taxes exempt from state spending limits on or after Jan. 1, 2026 (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html#storylink=var-wtk) — a provision that could nullify Prop. 40. The board urged a “no” vote.
Prop. 42 is billed as a safeguard for 401(k) accounts and personal property, but the board called it a “poison pill” designed to derail the billionaire wealth tax (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166989.html#storylink=var-wtk) in Prop. 40. If Prop. 42 gets more yes votes than Prop. 40, Prop. 40 would not take effect. Vote “no,” the board said.
Prop. 43 would raise the threshold to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives from a simple majority to 66.7% (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316956235.html#storylink=var-wtk), giving a 33.3% minority the power to block measures funding fire, police, flood control and other local services. The board opposed it and urged a “no” vote.
Prop. 44, the Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act, would require federally qualified health centers to spend at least 90% of revenue on patient services (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317472706.html#storylink=var-wtk), up from the roughly 80% most currently report. The board recommended a “no” vote, citing warnings the mandate could force clinics serving nearly 7 million patients to close.
Prop. 45 would reshape the California Environmental Quality Act (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317475362.html#storylink=var-wtk) by tightening deadlines, limiting public-comment periods and barring judges from halting entire projects over partial violations. The board endorsed a “yes” vote, arguing CEQA has too often been used to block needed housing.

content.thinking:
Checking McClatchy's yes and Mercury News' no reasoning more carefully. Also looking for full editorials from the Sacramento Bee or LA Times.

Enough information gathered. The vote removes a legal ban and sets minimum conditions without spending money on campaigns. Future programs would require separate political decisions.

The strongest argument against the measure is that it creates an incomplete permission structure. It allows officials to create programs by ordinance without another public vote. It lacks independent enforcement and meaningful caps on subsidies. Public money could stack on special-interest money. Several editorial boards that agree with the underlying concern still oppose it.

The strongest argument for yes is that the ban itself is the binding constraint blocking good programs. Charter cities already experiment with these laws, but the ban arbitrarily prevents everyone else from doing so. Specific statewide programs failed at the ballot because they included tax increases and one-size-fits-all designs. An opt-in enabling law is the correct institutional response to that history.

The measure includes stronger guardrails than opponents claim. It bans loan repayments and legal defense spending. It sets a $10 small-dollar limit. It protects against earmarks. It mandates spending limits and nondiscrimination.

Voluntary public financing is one of the few constitutional tools left in a post-Citizens United world.

The League of Women Voters, Common Cause, and Clean Money Campaign support it. McClatchy and the LA Times Skelton also say yes.

A no vote preserves a system where only personal wealth and large donors fund campaigns. That is worse than the risk of some poorly designed local programs.

The recommendation is yes. A failed vote would leave the statewide ban intact, and poorly designed programs could not be repealed locally. Charter cities are already exempt from that ban.

About 125 of California's 482 cities are charter cities. Most local governments are general law and remain banned. Counties are also prohibited from using public funds for campaigns.

The LAO and AG summaries disagree on whether charter counties are exempt from the ban. The LAO cites only certain charter cities, while the AG summary includes counties. The Johnson v. Bradley ruling applies home rule protections to charter cities but not to counties.

If only charter cities are exempt, counties would remain banned. County offices and state offices receive heavy special interest funding. This is a major concern. I will verify whether charter counties are also exempt.

I am also checking whether the measure's trigger mechanism is constitutional. I will verify whether its flaws are fatal enough to warrant a rejection. My leaning remains yes. The expected value of passing is moderate: several cities and possibly the state would experiment with well-designed small-donor match programs.

Clean Money and Common Cause would push for sound designs, and existing programs would serve as models. Some cities might still create weak or captured programs. Nondiscrimination rules and spending limits would constrain the worst abuses. Bad programs could be defunded by future budgets because they are not constitutional entitlements.

The measure does not appropriate a fixed sum. A bad program is reversible by the same body that created it, or by voters via referendum or initiative.

Passing would let more non-wealthy candidates run, strengthen small-donor power, and allow voluntary spending limits that are otherwise unconstitutional to impose. It would also reduce dependence on large donors in participating races.

A no vote preserves the status quo where billionaire self-funders and independent expenditure committees dominate. Qualified non-wealthy candidates stay out of races. Charter cities keep their programs, but everyone else remains blocked from experimentation.

The "wait for a better measure" strategy has failed for 38 years. A no vote is not a vote for reform; it is a vote to preserve the ban. The measure locks in permission rather than spending, so wasteful programs can be ended without another statewide constitutional fight.

The option value of lifting the ban outweighs keeping it. Bad programs can be ended locally, while good ones are currently impossible outside charter cities.

The Chronicle's call to study first is weak. Existing charter city programs have been available for decades without study. Waiting for a study that nobody is commissioning is a reason to delay forever. Studying those programs does not require maintaining the ban on new ones.

The blank check argument is overstated. A yes vote only authorizes future appropriations that would still go through normal budget processes, and existing local programs are modest. The lack of independent enforcement remains the strongest anti-argument, but it is not decisive.

The PRA's disclosure rules still apply to public campaign funds. The FPPC retains enforcement authority over contribution limits and prohibitions in 85300(a)-(d) and (g)-(h). It only excuses itself from administering local public financing systems. A candidate who uses public funds for legal defense would violate the PRA. Local prosecutors, civil litigants, and local ethics bodies can enforce that prohibition.

Opposition claims that the measure lacks spending limits, strict criteria, or that it would drain school and public safety funds are incorrect. The text explicitly requires expenditure limits and defines the $10 small-donor threshold. Earmarked funds are prohibited, and any general fund tradeoffs would be a local choice rather than a mandate.

Opposition claims that thousands of candidates will automatically receive money are incorrect; the measure only authorizes future programs and requires local qualification. The argument that it allows special interest money is misleading because the current system already permits such funding, and matching systems are designed to work alongside limited private contributions.

Supporter overclaims should be rejected. The claim that elections will be "won not bought" is overstated because independent expenditure committees and self-funding remain possible. The "$1 per resident" figure is marketing hyperbole rather than a binding cap.

The URL points to the 2026 public financing measure, not a 2024 climate bond. The recommendation remains yes.

I considered a steelman argument for no: public financing only works if private money is replaced by tightly capped public funds with strong enforcement, and Prop 4 does not lock that in. I rejected it. The recommendation remains yes.

The measure authorizes additive public subsidies with caps and qualification rules written by beneficiaries, enforced by nobody in particular. Empirical evidence shows that poorly designed programs do not reduce donor influence. California's track record of interest-group capture makes this especially risky. The Legislature had the opportunity to propose a specific, capped, independently administered program, but chose a blank permission structure instead because voters reject specific programs.

The measure is not a true laboratory of democracy. It avoids voter accountability for program costs. Voters have rejected similar proposals three times. The foreign-money penalty is a Trojan sweetener. Former FPPC chairs oppose the measure. Multiple editorial boards, including the Chronicle, also oppose it.

The no vote is fiscally responsible and institutionally careful. A better measure would require independent administration, minimum small-donor thresholds, capped public subsidies, and mandatory rejection of large contributions. The choice is between Prop 4 and the ban, not between this measure and a hypothetical ideal.

The ideal program is not on the ballot and is unlikely to appear, given prior rejections. A no vote would kill reform by demanding perfection. The measure is a floor, not a ceiling. Implementing statutes and ordinances can add strong safeguards after passage. Cities can still adopt well-designed local systems.

The Chronicle's call for both maximum local freedom and mandated best practices is internally inconsistent. Lange's approach of maximum freedom is consistent with the measure's theory.

The risk that jurisdictions will choose bad designs is mitigated by annual budget visibility, reversibility, and existing models to copy.

The recommendation remains yes.

The SF Chronicle, the most sophisticated local policy voice, voted no. That carries significant weight.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)

The influence of money on political races has gotten out of control, but allowing candidates to accept public funds — taxpayer dollars — for campaign purposes is not the answer.
We recommend voting “no” on Proposition 4. Our tax dollars should not be spent on election campaigns.

Endorsement: Reject San Mateo Community College District’s $848 million Measure V (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-reject-san-mateo-community-college-districts-848-million-measure-v/)

Sky-high spending
Consider this news organization’s report last week (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/11/whos-donating-to-the-billionaire-backed-group-has-raised-almost-300-million-to-fight-the-wealth-tax/) showing how a single political action committee backed by billionaires — Building a Better California — has spent nearly a quarter of a billion dollars this year alone, breaking all previous records.
Understandably alarmed, this inundation of money into state politics has pushed legislators to ask voters this November to repeal a 1988 law and allow taxpayer dollars to be spent on campaigns.
A “yes” vote would allow state and local governments to create programs so that public funds — again, taxpayer dollars — could be set aside for election campaigns.
We understand the desire to take corporate money out of elections.
This year’s race for California governor (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/california-governor-contributions-takeaways/) highlights that need more than ever. A political spending committee comprising the state realtors association, California Chamber of Commerce, Pacific Gas & Electric and the state electrical workers union spent a record $32 million on ads opposing Democratic billionaire Tom Steyer, who ultimately placed third in the primary.
Leading into those primaries, Democratic nominee Xavier Becerra — whose name appears on the Nov. 3 ballot — was backed by Meta, AirBnB and Uber at $1 million each and Chevron, McDonalds and DaVita at $500,000 each, to name a few.
Those corporate dollars force the fair question: If elected, how confident are we that Becerra will have the people’s interests at heart, and not those corporations’?
Not solution
Many counties are already struggling financially. Some have placed sales tax measures on the ballot this year to bring more revenue into their general funds. Some already had sales tax measures on the ballot in 2024. And some still face a budget deficit. Other counties may be sitting on the fence, but there is no wiggle room in their budgets to create a fund for campaign financing.
Moreover, people should be able to decide if they want their money to go toward supporting a candidate. Our elected officials should not make that decision for us — especially if they are up for re-election.
We agree that special interests should not be able to buy candidates or campaigns, but Proposition 4 is not the answer. Creating a fund of taxpayer dollars and making it available for election campaigns is not the answer. Those hard-earned dollars belong in a municipality’s general fund, to be used on improving roadways, funding for public safety officers or enhancing our local parks.
Reject Proposition 4.

McClatchy Media’s endorsements for all 14 propositions on California’s ballot
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
Updated October 27, 2026 9:16 AM
The California state Capitol on Aug. 31, 2026.
Lauren Chapman
lchapman@sacbee.com
Opinion journalists for McClatchy Media conducted interviews with supporters and opponents of all 14 statewide propositions on your November ballot. The journalists then deliberated and decided how they would vote on each one, just as voters do. Their endorsements, linked below, explain their positions.
What to Know
Here are key takeaways:
Prop. 1 would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds for affordable housing and CalVet home loans (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317326136.html#storylink=var-wtk), with $10 billion aimed at closing financing gaps for nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes already in the pipeline. The board endorsed a “yes” vote but urged the state to publish a transparent dashboard tracking costs and results.
Prop. 2 would raise California’s rainy day fund cap from 10% to 20% (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317091637.html#storylink=var-wtk) of annual tax collections and allow some reserves to pay down state debts, including $20 billion still owed to the federal government for pandemic-era unemployment borrowing. The board recommended a “yes” vote as a safeguard against future downturns.
Prop. 3 would make permanent a tax on California’s top 2% of earners (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317445836.html#storylink=var-wtk) — single filers making at least $361,000 and joint filers at least $721,000 — that generates between $5 billion and $15 billion a year for schools and community colleges. The board endorsed a “yes” vote.
Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on public financing of state and local campaigns (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317448027.html#storylink=var-wtk), allowing matching-fund or public-grant programs for qualifying candidates. The board backed a “yes” vote, arguing public financing reduces reliance on wealthy donors.
Prop. 5 would eliminate the second question on recall ballots asking who should replace an ousted official (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316911387.html#storylink=var-wtk), instead triggering special elections or gubernatorial appointments. The board strongly endorsed a “yes” vote, noting past recalls have installed replacements with less voter support than the official removed.
Prop. 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to finance second mortgages (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317470188.html#storylink=var-wtk) covering up to 17% of a new home’s price for middle-class buyers. Despite reservations about default risk, the board recommended a “yes” vote.
Prop. 38 proposes an $8.4 billion bond for immunology research (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166634.html#storylink=var-wtk), with half guaranteed to an institute tied to UCLA and backed by billionaire physician Gary K. Michelson. The board urged a “no” vote, warning the measure would exempt the institute from public-records laws.
Prop. 39 would require government-issued ID at the polls and partial ID numbers on mail ballots (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317017898.html#storylink=var-wtk), with backers including nine billionaires tracked by Forbes. The board recommended a “no” vote, warning the measure would disenfranchise more legitimate voters than it would stop fraudulent ones.
Prop. 40 would impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on Californians worth more than $1 billion (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317269166.html#storylink=var-wtk), with 90% of proceeds reserved for healthcare amid federal Medi-Cal cuts projected to cost 1.3 million residents coverage by 2030. A majority of the board endorsed a “yes” vote.
Prop. 41 is a constitutional amendment backed by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other wealthy donors that would ban taxes exempt from state spending limits on or after Jan. 1, 2026 (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html#storylink=var-wtk) — a provision that could nullify Prop. 40. The board urged a “no” vote.
Prop. 42 is billed as a safeguard for 401(k) accounts and personal property, but the board called it a “poison pill” designed to derail the billionaire wealth tax (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166989.html#storylink=var-wtk) in Prop. 40. If Prop. 42 gets more yes votes than Prop. 40, Prop. 40 would not take effect. Vote “no,” the board said.
Prop. 43 would raise the threshold to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives from a simple majority to 66.7% (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316956235.html#storylink=var-wtk), giving a 33.3% minority the power to block measures funding fire, police, flood control and other local services. The board opposed it and urged a “no” vote.
Prop. 44, the Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act, would require federally qualified health centers to spend at least 90% of revenue on patient services (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317472706.html#storylink=var-wtk), up from the roughly 80% most currently report. The board recommended a “no” vote, citing warnings the mandate could force clinics serving nearly 7 million patients to close.
Prop. 45 would reshape the California Environmental Quality Act (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317475362.html#storylink=var-wtk) by tightening deadlines, limiting public-comment periods and barring judges from halting entire projects over partial violations. The board endorsed a “yes” vote, arguing CEQA has too often been used to block needed housing.
The summary points above were compiled with the help of AI tools and edited by journalists. The source reporting referenced above was written and edited entirely by journalists.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
I have enough information to decide.

I will vote yes. The measure is an enabling statute, not an appropriation. The current ban arbitrarily blocks most counties and cities from exploring public financing. Only about 121 charter cities are allowed to experiment with it.

The 1988 ban specifically blocked Sacramento County's local experiment. Empirical evidence supports small-donor matching and vouchers, models already used in California cities. Prop 4's criteria align with these existing approaches.

Prop 4 steers toward small-donor matching and vouchers rather than unlimited grants. It requires broad-based support and spending limits. Opponents' claims are overstated. The measure does not provide blank checks. It protects earmarked funds and bans using public money for legal defense or personal loans.

The measure has implementation weaknesses. It lacks an independent enforcement mandate and a numeric floor for broad-based support. Caps are set later, and local programs may coexist with private money. The FPPC is not required to enforce local programs. Definitional sections can be amended by two-thirds vote.

These are watchful implementation concerns rather than reasons to keep the blanket ban. Implementing laws can add protections. Bad programs are budget decisions that can be reversed. The current ban cannot be reversed locally.

Prior rejections targeted specific costly statewide programs with dedicated taxes, not local options. The Legislature explicitly notes this distinction.

Good-government organizations with subject-matter expertise support the measure. Taxpayer associations oppose it on principle against any public campaign spending.

PROP
4
REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Repeals prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety. Fiscal Impact: Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs. Supporters: League of Women Voters of CA; California Nurses Association; Mental Health Advocacy; Social Security Works; Consumer Watchdog Opponents: California Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; Family Business Assn of California; United Latinos Action
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs for public office candidates, subject to limits on which public funds could be used, how the public funds could be used, and who could receive them.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: State and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign finance programs for public office candidates.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES ON 4. California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns— communities in all other 49 states have this right. Special interests want to keep the ban to protect their power. Prop. 4 removes it. Strict taxpayer safeguards. Vote YES: Elections should be won, not bought.
CON
Prop. 4 allows politicians to use YOUR taxpayer money to fund their negative campaigns. Prop. 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money they can get. Worse yet, Prop. 4 allows SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY IN POLITICS. NO ON PROP. 4.

PROP
4
REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
The Political Reform Act. Many people, groups, and businesses spend money to support or oppose candidates for public office and ballot measures. California's Political Reform Act sets rules for how money can be used in politics and requires public reporting of political spending. These rules apply to state and local candidates, ballot measures, and other public officials, but not to federal candidates or officials. (Federal law establishes campaign finance and reporting requirements for federal offices.) The Political Reform Act has been updated by voters over the years.
Ban on Public Funds to Pay for Campaigns. The Political Reform Act bans the use of public funds for political candidates' campaigns. This ban applies to most elected offices at the state level and local level. (This ban does not apply to city office elections in certain charter cities. Los Angeles, San Francisco, Long Beach, Oakland, and Berkeley are current examples of charter cities that provide public funds to certain campaigns.)
Entities That Oversee Campaign Finance Laws. California's campaign finance laws are administered by the Fair Political Practices Commission and the California Secretary of State. State law requires people and groups to report how much money they give, receive, and spend on political campaigns. This information is available to the public on the Secretary of State's website. The Fair Political Practices Commission enforces and interprets the Political Reform Act. The Fair Political Practices Commission reviews the finance reports and can fine candidates and donors who break the law. The Fair Political Practices Commission issues guidance based on its interpretation of the Political Reform Act.
PROPOSAL
Lifts Ban on Use of Public Funds to Pay for Candidates' Campaigns. Proposition 4 lifts the ban on using public funds for political candidates' campaigns. Removing the ban allows state and local governments to create public campaign financing programs in the future if they wish. Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance system for the state or local governments directly.
Sets Rules for Future State and Local Public Campaign Finance Programs. Proposition 4 sets broad rules for future state and local public campaign finance programs but leaves many key design decisions to future state and local decision makers. Proposition 4 limits which public funds can be used for campaigns, who can receive the funds, and how the funds can be spent in any future public campaign finance program. For example, money meant for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used for campaigns. Candidates can only receive public funds if they show broad-based support in their district and agree to spending limits and other program rules. Public funds cannot be used for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate's personal campaign loan. State and local governments can design and implement their own programs within the broad rules set by Proposition 4.
Fair Political Practices Commission Would Issue Guidance on Public Campaign Finance Programs. Proposition 4 specifies that the Fair Political Practices Commission is not required to administer or enforce local public campaign finance programs. Rather, state and local government officials could ask the Fair Political Practices Commission for guidance on how to create public campaign finance programs consistent with Proposition 4.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Costs of Possible Public Campaign Finance Programs Depend on Future Decisions. Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance program. However, it allows state and local governments to create such programs in the future. The cost of these programs could be significant for governments that choose to create them. The total cost would depend on which governments created such programs and how those programs were designed.
Minor State Costs to Support State and Local Governments Considering Public Campaign Finance Programs. If voters approve Proposition 4, state and local government officials likely would ask the Fair Political Practices Commission for guidance on creating public campaign finance programs under the Political Reform Act. This likely would require the Fair Political Practices Commission to hire more legal staff to help answer these questions. As a result, state costs would be a few hundred thousand dollars each year. This amount is much less than one-tenth of 1 percent (0.1 percent) of the state's total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)
Visit sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/cal-access-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/cal-access-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals) for a list of committees primarily formed to support or oppose this measure.

4
REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 4
YES ON PROPOSITION 4, THE CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT: ELECTIONS SHOULD BE WON, NOT BOUGHT
The amount of money in California elections is outrageous; it's distorting our democracy. Since 2020, more than $1 billion has been spent on California state candidate races alone. This massive spending gives special interests greater access and influence while drowning out the voices of ordinary Californians.
PROP. 4 HELPS QUALIFIED CANDIDATES COMPETE
Running for office today often requires either personal wealth or access to wealthy donors. Deep pockets have become an unofficial requirement to run for office, leaving too many qualified candidates behind.
PROP. 4 CHANGES THE WAY WE FINANCE ELECTION CAMPAIGNS
Programs like small-dollar donation matching help candidates compete without relying on wealthy donors. However, most California communities are banned from using these tools, allowing the influence of big money to grow.
Proposition 4 lifts that ban, giving voters and local governments the option to adopt public financing with strict safeguards so qualified candidates-regardless of their income-can compete against candidates who are backed by wealthy interests.
PROP. 4 BUILDS ON A PROVEN MODEL
We know this reform works because it's working in other states. Thousands of candidates from different backgrounds have been elected in fourteen states and 26 localities using similar systems. They are new people with good ideas from all walks of life. Because they don't rely on wealthy donors, they can speak their mind and work for the people, not the special interests.
PROP. 4 GIVES LOCAL COMMUNITIES A CHOICE
Proposition 4 does not create a public financing program. It simply gives local governments the option to adopt one if they choose.
If a community does, the cost is as little as $1 per resident each year-a small investment to help counter the billions spent influencing California's elections.
PROP. 4 PROTECTS TAXPAYERS
Taxpayer Safeguards:
Requires candidates to meet strict eligibility criteria and abide by spending limits to qualify for public funds.
Prohibits public funding from favoring incumbents or discriminating based on political party.
Prohibits the use of public funds for legal defense or fines.
PROP. 4 CRACKS DOWN ON ILLEGAL FOREIGN MONEY
Proposition 4 triples the maximum fines for illegal foreign campaign contributions and expenditures, strengthening penalties for those who attempt to interfere in California's elections.
PROP. 4 IS SUPPORTED BY LEADERS ACROSS CALIFORNIA
Proposition 4 is backed by a broad coalition including League of Women Voters of California, California Nurses Association, Mental Health Advocacy Services, Social Security Works, California Clean Money Campaign, California Common Cause, California National Organization for Women, Californians for Disability Rights, Consumer Watchdog, Courage California, Democracy for America, Indivisible California: Statestrong, La Defensa, Money Out Voters In, Voters Right to Know, and many others.
PROP. 4 GIVES CALIFORNIANS THE OPPORTUNITY TO RECLAIM THEIR ELECTIONS and ensure they reflect the values of the people, not just the wealthiest donors.
YES ON 4-Restore power to voters, not wealthy donors
Lorrel Plimier , Co-President
League of Women Voters of California
Catherine Kennedy , President
California Nurses Association
Tom Umberg , California State Senator
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 4
Here is what the politicians supporting Proposition 4 do not tell you:
Proposition 4 REPEALS the voter-approved law that PROHIBITS candidates from using taxpayer money to run for office.
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money. In the election last June, more than 60 candidates ran for Governor. Proposition 4 would allow thousands of candidates to get taxpayer money!

REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Current law prohibits state and local governments from using public funds for election campaigns except in charter cities and counties.
This measure repeals that prohibition and allows state and local governments to establish public campaign financing programs for candidates who agree to specified spending limits and meet eligibility criteria.
Prohibits public funding programs from using funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety.
Prohibits candidates from using public funds for legal defense costs, fines, or repayment of personal loans to campaigns.
Triples maximum fine for campaign contributions by foreign entities.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs.

Proposition 4 repeals the 1988 ban on public campaign funding. It does not create a program itself. State and local governments could establish one later. Funds cannot be used for education, transportation, or public safety.

Candidates must show broad-based support and accept spending limits. Public funds cannot cover legal defense, fines, or personal loans. The measure prohibits discrimination based on party or incumbent status. It also triples maximum fines for illegal foreign campaign contributions. The state budget impact is small. Actual program costs would depend on future decisions. Charter cities already have similar programs. Voters previously rejected similar measures twice.

Supporters include the League of Women Voters, Common Cause, and Consumer Watchdog. Opponents include the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, CalTax, and the San Francisco Chronicle editorial board. California is the only state that bans public campaign financing. The 1988 ban was partly struck down by courts but remains in effect.

Over $1 billion has been spent on state candidate races since 2020. The measure does not force any jurisdiction to spend money; it only removes a prohibition and sets guardrails. Charter cities already have this option, creating an uneven system for general law cities and counties. Evidence from other jurisdictions suggests public financing can increase candidate diversity, reduce donor influence, and increase small-donor participation.

Public financing is the main constitutional mechanism to secure voluntary spending limits under Buckley v. Valeo. The measure also provides a small penalty increase for foreign campaign contributions and protects funds for education, transportation, and public safety. Opponents worry it gives politicians a blank check to design systems that benefit themselves.

The measure leaves hard caps and candidate eligibility rules to future politicians. It does not bar candidates from accepting private contributions, so public funds might simply supplement them rather than replace them. Research on similar programs is mixed; some studies show limited effects, and public financing often suffers from underfunding or gaming. Outside spending remains uncontrolled, which can undermine the program's intended impact.

SECTION 1. This act shall be known, and may be

SEC. 2. The Legislature finds and declares all of the
following:
(a) All citizens should be able to make their voices

4 (b) Elections for local or state elective office should be
fair, open, and competitive.
(c) The increasing costs of political campaigns can
force candidates to rely on large contributions from
wealthy donors and special interests, which can give
those wealthy donors and special interests

(d) Such disproportionate influence can undermine

(e) Special interests contribute more to incumbents
than challengers because they seek access to elected
officials, and such contributions account for a large
portion of the financial incumbency advantage, as
confirmed by studies such as those published in the
Journal of Politics in 2014 and Political Research
Quarterly in 2016.
(f) Citizen-funded election programs, in which
qualified candidates can receive public funds for the
purpose of communicating with voters rather than
relying exclusively on private donors, are currently
operative in five charter cities in California, as well as
numerous other local and state jurisdictions.
(g) Citizen-funded election programs encourage
competition by reducing the financial advantages of
incumbency and making it possible for citizens from all
walks of life, not only those with connections to wealthy
donors or special interests, to run for office, as
confirmed by studies such as those published in State
Politics and Policy Quarterly in 2008, and by the
Campaign Finance Institute in 2015, the National
Institute on Money in State Politics in 2016, and the
State Politics and Policy Quarterly in 2022.
(h) By reducing reliance on wealthy donors and special
interests, citizen-funded election programs inhibit
improper practices, protect against corruption or the
appearance of corruption, and protect the political
integrity of our governmental institutions.
(i) In Johnson v. Bradley (1992) 4 Cal.4th 389, the
California Supreme Court highlighted the Court of
Appeal’s observation that “it seems obvious that public
money reduces rather than increases the fund raising
pressures on public office seekers and thereby reduces
the undue influence of special interest groups.”

In summary
Prop. 4 would lift a ban that prohibits state and most local candidates from using public funding for their political campaigns. Proponents argue the mechanism helps more candidates run for office, but opponents are skeptical.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
In 1988, a Democrat, a Republican and an independent in the state Legislature co-authored a ballot measure to ban most political campaigns from using public money.
Their rationale? There was already too much money in politics.
“It certainly makes no sense to open the biggest money source of all, the taxpayers’ purses and wallets,” proponents argued (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1988&context=ca_ballot_props). Nearly 60% of voters agreed.
Almost four decades later, some good-government groups argue that the state needs to do the exact opposite to counter the influence of money in politics.
They, along with the state Democratic Party, are backing Proposition 4 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-4-public-fundraising/) on the November ballot, which would lift the 1988 ban and authorize the state and most local governments to set up public campaign financing systems for state and local races.
Seven charter cities in California, including San Francisco, Berkeley and Oakland, were spared from the 1988 ban and already have public campaign financing.
To qualify for the funding, candidates must meet criteria such as proving they have a certain number of small donors or agreeing to cap how much they raise and spend on their campaign. Depending on the city, eligible candidates receive the funding as a grant, a matching fund indexed to their total donations, or a voucher voters can give to campaigns.
Proponents of Prop. 4 may face an uphill battle: Voters have twice rejected similar ballot measures to lift the ban, and public polling so far suggests voters are skeptical.
What supporters, opponents say
Elections have gotten more expensive over the past three decades, both federally and statewide.
In 2000, federal candidates, parties and special interests spent $5.6 billion on congressional and presidential races. By 2020, that number had nearly quadrupled to $18 billion (https://www.opensecrets.org/elections-overview/cost-of-election?display=T), according to OpenSecrets, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit that tracks campaign spending nationwide.
In California, special interests spent $26 million (https://calmatters.org/politics/2025/10/prop50-money-ads-mailers-billboards/) running competing ads on redistricting last year, making it the most expensive ballot measure race in state history. This year, California had the most expensive governor’s race (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/03/us/elections/california-governor-campaign-finance.html) in U.S. history, with billionaire Tom Steyer pouring $213 million (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-rich-candidates-funding-elections/) of his own money into his unsuccessful gubernatorial bid.
Supporters of Prop. 4 say public campaign financing is necessary as a check against that kind of unfettered private campaign spending, because candidates often must accept campaign spending limits to qualify for public funding. They say public financing will lead to more diverse candidates by attracting those who otherwise couldn’t afford to run for office.
