“We need to change the way we finance election campaigns so candidates can run and win without having to raise big money, and they can spend their time listening to voters rather than their donors,” said Trent Lange, president of California Clean Money Campaign and co-chair of the Yes on Prop. 4 campaign.
Gov. Gavin Newsom (https://calmatters.org/tag/gavin-newsom/) and the Democratic-led state Legislature, which voted last year (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb42) to place Prop. 4 on the November ballot, also support the measure. Sen. Tom Umberg (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/thomas-umberg-165043), a Santa Ana Democrat and a co-author of Prop. 4, said it would help alleviate a “growing cynicism in politics” and allow candidates to spend more time developing policies instead of fundraising.
“To the extent that we can engage particularly small donors, that will … empower and also engage the body politic, particularly young people,” he said.
But opponents say politicians should not use taxpayer dollars (https://caltax.org/prop4/) to run campaigns. They argue the measure would force voters to subsidize candidates they otherwise wouldn’t support, and that fraudulent candidates could exploit the system.
Voters have previously rejected ballot initiatives that would have allowed public money to be used for political campaigns. Nearly two-thirds of voters shot down a 2000 measure that would have allowed candidates to tap public funds for advertising (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2000/25_03_2000.html). In 2010, 58% of voters opposed a 2010 measure (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_15,_Biennial_Lobbyist_Fee_and_Public_Campaign_Funding_Measure_(June_2010)) to lift the 1988 ban.
“The voters have been quite clear they don’t want taxpayer money being used for politics,” Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican, said last year (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/278290#t=221&f=fe479f37ee7a3df6888379e9be069fd8) on the Assembly floor. “Unfortunately, politicians simply can’t take no for an answer.”

Critics also doubt the effectiveness of Prop. 4, arguing it is not specific enough to have teeth.
Prop. 4 offers only broad instructions to local governments and the state. It would ban candidates from using public funds meant for education, public safety and transportation. It would require candidates to prove they have enough public support and to agree to certain spending limits to receive funding, but doesn’t spell out how much. It would also ban candidates from using the money to pay for legal defenses, fines or personal loans to their campaigns.
The measure specifically exempts the Fair Political Practices Commission, the state’s campaign finance watchdog, from ensuring local programs are not exploited or abused, leaving it largely to local governments. But not every local government has its own watchdog agency, let alone an effective one.
The San Francisco Chronicle’s editorial board, in opposing Prop. 4, argued that its rules “are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop. 4 offers no guarantee they will be.”
Effectiveness debate
Fifteen states and Washington, D.C., offer some sort of statewide public financing for political campaigns, according to an analysis by the National Conference of State Legislatures (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/public-financing-of-campaigns-overview).
Studies are mixed on the effectiveness of those programs.
Some, including one in 2003 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1532673X03256784) by two University of Maryland scholars, suggest that candidates who accept public financing spend less time fundraising, freeing them up for other campaign activities.
Some researchers found that public financing expanded the pool of candidates running for office. A 2022 study of Seattle’s program (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0047272722000780), which gives each registered voter four $25 vouchers to contribute to the campaign of their choice, concluded that the program boosted the number of candidates by 86%. Another study (https://web.stanford.edu/~neilm/The%20Impact%20of%20Public%20Financing%20on%20Electoral%20Competition.pdf) of Arizona and Maine’s programs found that they “significantly increased competition.”
Others disagreed. The United States Government Accountability Office, the nonpartisan research agency advising Congress, studied Arizona and Maine’s programs (https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-10-390.pdf) in 2010 and concluded there was no evidence that public financing led to more candidates.
There’s little evidence that public financing has curbed the influence of private donors, according to the Seattle study and the GAO report.
In California, few studies have examined the effectiveness of local programs. A 2023 San Francisco Ethics Commission study found candidates have increasingly tapped into the public funds and that third-party spending was “at near all-time lows.” But the commission encouraged a more comprehensive analysis. A 2013 study (https://www.oaklandca.gov/files/assets/city/v/3/boards-amp-commissions/documents/pec/publications/reports-by-third-parties/2013-05-01-evaluating-oaklands-limited-public-financing-act.pdf) in Oakland found no evidence its program diluted the influence of wealthy donors, although it did seem to boost competition.
Researchers point to the difficulty (https://sgp.jhu.edu/primers/public-funding-of-us-elections/#conclusion) of studying public financing programs, because most apply in only a handful of states and it is hard to measure what would have happened if the programs had not been in place.
The lack of compelling evidence makes Prop. 4 proponents’ claims shaky, the San Diego Union-Tribune’s editorial board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/04/endorsement-dont-buy-prop-4s-baloney-about-publicly-financed-campaigns/) argued.
“So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits,” it said.
The ballot measure should not be overly prescriptive, said Dora Rose, deputy director for the League of Women Voters of California, a co-sponsor of Prop. 4.
“Prop. 4 sets basic safeguards and then lets communities learn from the evidence and decide what works for them,” she said.
For now, voters appear skeptical. A September poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the Public Policy Institute of California found 53% of likely voters would oppose Prop. 4, while just 42% would vote yes. Another poll (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf) by the UC-Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies shows a tighter matchup, with 35% of likely voters supporting the measure and another 35% against it.

Endorsement: California hasn’t even bothered to study its existing public financing programs. No on Prop 4
Proposition 4 would overturn California’s ban on public financing of campaigns but does not include key guardrails.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 6, 2026
Americans don’t agree on much in today’s hyperpolarized climate. But they overwhelmingly believe that money is a corrupting influence in politics.
According to a 2023 Pew Research poll (https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/09/19/the-biggest-problems-and-greatest-strengths-of-the-u-s-political-system/), 85% of respondents said they thought the cost of mounting a campaign deters “good people” from running for office, and 84% said wealthy special interests and lobbyists exercise too much sway over politics.
Unfortunately, systemic reform to our campaign finance system is incredibly difficult. The 2010 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Citizens United struck down limits on independent political spending by corporations and labor unions.
But could California carve its own path to reducing money in politics?

That’s what backers of Proposition 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which Democratic state lawmakers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) placed on the November ballot, contend their measure will do.
Prop 4 would overturn California’s ban on public campaign financing — in place since voters approved Prop 73 in 1988 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_73,_Funds_for_Election_Campaigns_Initiative_(June_1988)) — and give local and state governments the option of providing taxpayer funding for candidates’ political campaigns.
Supporters argue this will dilute the influence of special interests while making elected officials more accountable to voters — and leveling the playing field and encouraging more diverse, nonincumbent and first-time candidates.
That certainly sounds good, but is there meaningful research to back it up?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A natural place to look is California’s charter cities, which are exempt from the public financing ban; seven have programs (https://www.commoncause.org/california/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/CA-Municipal-Index-Reportv7-Final_Authored.pdf). San Francisco, Berkeley, Los Angeles, Sacramento and Long Beach provide matching funds to eligible candidates who receive a certain level of small-dollar donations; Oakland gives residents “democracy vouchers” they can donate to candidates and Richmond offers grants to candidates each time they reach a new fundraising tier.
How well have these programs been working?
Unfortunately, no one really knows. There hasn’t been much academic research into any of the programs, let alone a rigorous cross-comparison of them.
Despite a wealth of information on San Francisco’s public financing program — captured in an annual report from the city ethics commission — the data has yet to be thoroughly studied. Indeed, the overworked commission refers to its report as “primarily descriptive” (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2023/05/san-francisco-public-campaign-financing-program-report-november-8-2022-election.html) and practically begs for a “more comprehensive analysis” of the program — noting that (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2025/03/san-francisco-public-campaign-financing-program-report-for-the-november-5-2024-election.html) certain “labor-intensive” and “paperwork-heavy” aspects are “ineffective.”
Meanwhile, the studies that do exist suggest there’s a lot of room for improvement.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A 2013 examination of Oakland’s program (https://www.oaklandca.gov/files/assets/city/v/3/boards-amp-commissions/documents/pec/publications/reports-by-third-parties/2013-05-01-evaluating-oaklands-limited-public-financing-act.pdf) found “no evidence” that it reduced the influence of wealthy donors, spurred more candidates to run or increased voter turnout, although it appears to have made certain races more competitive and shrunk incumbents’ margin of victory. And a 2017 peer-reviewed study (https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/for-2017-0015/html) comparing New York City’s and Los Angeles’ public financing programs found that L.A.’s program design made it “substantially less effective” than New York’s.
All available research indicates that the effectiveness of a public campaign finance program depends enormously on how it’s designed.
Yet Prop 4 ignores best practices and imposes no meaningful checks on bad policies.
It gives local and state governments broad discretion to design programs, as long as they follow a few basic rules: To receive public funds, candidates would have to demonstrate “broad-based” community support — such as receiving a certain amount of small-dollar donations — and agree to abide by spending limits. They couldn’t use public funds earmarked for education, transportation and public safety — or use public money to repay personal loans to their campaign or cover legal defense fees.
“Cities are the laboratory of democracy … We wanted to give maximum freedom to jurisdictions,” Trent Lange, executive director of the California Clean Money Action Fund and co-chair of the Yes on Prop 4 campaign, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But we’ve been running these experiments for years. The labs are in operation, but no one has bothered to gather the data or review the research.
And we have significant concerns about letting state and local governments run wild with taxpayer money — especially in the dark.
True, Prop 4 has some protections. The ban on using public funds to pay legal defense fees, for example, is aimed at closing the Eric Swalwell loophole: The disgraced Democratic ex-U.S. representative used hundreds of thousands of dollars from his California gubernatorial campaign (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/eric-swalwell-campaign-payments-22362761.php) to pay for his legal defense against multiple sexual-assault allegations.
But such protections are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop 4 offers no guarantee they will be.
In fact, it explicitly exempts the state’s respected campaign finance watchdog, the California Fair Political Practices Commission, from administering or enforcing local public financing programs.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Nor does the measure require local governments to set up their own watchdog agencies — even though Lange acknowledged “a public financing system needs a good oversight board.”
That’s a recipe for disaster.
Without San Francisco’s ethics commission, for example, 2024 mayoral candidate Mark Farrell — who received $1.2 million in public funds (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2026/03/campaign-finance-audit-report-mark-farrell-for-mayor-2024-id-1466726.html) — might have gotten away with illegally using funds (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/mark-farrell-hit-ethics-fine-eve-of-mayor-election-19886013.php) from a separate ballot-measure campaign to subsidize his mayoral campaign (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/emilyhoeven/article/mark-farrell-campaign-finance-19654509.php).
We understand Prop 4 proponents’ hesitation to be overly prescriptive — San Francisco’s ridiculously clunky charter is the result of years of unnecessary regulations and stipulations being written into ballot measures.
But the details missing from Prop 4 aren’t ancillary. As the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office observed (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop4-110326.pdf), the measure leaves “many key design decisions” up to state and local lawmakers, who could directly benefit from the programs they create.
Consider the requirement that candidates abide by spending limits if they accept public funds. That sounds great, but Prop 4 doesn’t include guardrails for what a meaningful cap would be — and some local governments clearly need guardrails.
Thomas Hiltachk, a lawyer who frequently works on ballot measures and opposes Prop 4, cited the Los Angeles County city of Inglewood, which in 2020 capped local campaign contributions at the absurd amount of $100,000 per person (https://www.dailybreeze.com/2020/11/24/inglewood-caps-campaign-contributions-at-100000-to-avoid-new-state-law/) — 21 times the statewide max of $4,700.
This isn’t to say that public campaign financing is inherently a bad idea. We’ve supported the idea in the past (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Editorial-California-deserves-more-campaign-12165476.php), including a 2016 Berkeley pilot program (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-Yes-on-Measure-X1-9984435.php).
But we can’t get behind a measure that doesn’t require local and state governments to adhere to any established best practices. This is a fatal flaw that opens the door to limited taxpayer funds being wasted on efforts that don’t meaningfully move the needle — at a time of widespread budget deficits.

content.thinking:
I have a solid understanding of the measure.

Prop 4 repeals the ban on public financing without creating a new system. It would only establish minimum conditions for any future program, including restrictions on earmarked funds and strict candidate criteria.

The strict criteria would require broad-based support, such as small-dollar contributions or resident vouchers. The measure caps the largest contribution at $10 and prohibits requirements for signature counts or total dollar amounts exceeding $10 per contributor.

Opponents claim the measure lacks a definition for "strict criteria," but the text explicitly defines it. Candidates must demonstrate broad-based support through small-dollar contributions or resident vouchers, with the $10 cap and signature prohibition clearly specified.

The measure also bars public funds from covering legal defense or fines. It prevents candidates from repaying personal loans received with public money after the campaign ends. Programs must not discriminate by party or incumbent status.

The measure would require that funds be available to all qualified candidates for the same office without regard to incumbency or party. It also permits raising expenditure limits based on a formula tied to opponent's net supportive funds and independent expenditures. This "rescue" mechanism was partially struck down in Arizona Free Enterprise Club v. Bennett (2011).

The Arizona court found that matching funds tied to opponent spending violated the First Amendment by penalizing private speech. Prop 4 subdivision (f) authorizes raising expenditure limits for qualified candidates.

The formula caps the spending limit at the highest net supportive funds of any opponent for the same office, plus independent expenditures against the candidate, minus independent expenditures supporting them. This raises the spending cap based on opponent activity rather than providing additional public matching funds.

This approach is constitutionally sound. It raises the voluntary spending cap for publicly financed candidates when opponents spend more, rather than automatically providing extra public matching funds. The formula caps how much the limit can increase.

The FPPC would not be responsible for administering or enforcing local public financing programs. Local governments would handle enforcement instead, similar to current charter city programs. The FPPC would still enforce the Political Reform Act generally.

Subdivisions (e), (f), and (h) can be amended by a simple majority vote under the easier amendment standard. The core protections requiring no earmarked funds, spending limits, legal defense coverage, personal loan repayment restrictions, and non-discrimination would need a two-thirds vote to amend.

Re-examining the amendment standards reveals a potential contradiction. Subdivisions (e), (f), and (h) are restricted to voter approval, while the remaining subdivisions can be amended by a two-thirds vote. This reverses the typical pattern where easier amendments require less scrutiny.

The amendment standards are still ambiguous. Subdivisions (e), (f), and (h) may be restricted to voter approval, while the remaining protections could allow a two-thirds legislative vote. I need to examine the actual enrolled bill text and Section 81012 to resolve this.

The foreign money penalty would triple the maximum fine for contributions by foreign entities, though the minimum fine remains unchanged. This is a modest strengthening rather than a transformative anti-foreign-money provision.

Opponents' claims about unlimited candidate access and funding are accurate. The proposition itself contains no statewide cap on program size or individual spending limits. Future programs could still restrict candidates through qualification thresholds, but the enabling legislation does not create a funded program.

The proposition does not cap the dollar amount of public subsidies. Future programs would set those limits through their own statutes, ordinances, or charters. Opponents are correct that politicians determine the actual funding levels.

The claim that the measure imposes no spending limit is inaccurate. It requires candidates to comply with expenditure limits in order to qualify for public financing.

The proposition does not require candidates to actually qualify for the ballot. A future program could potentially provide public funding to unqualified candidates, though the measure itself only establishes broad-based support criteria.

The strict criteria bar on signature thresholds applies only to public-funding qualification, not to separate ballot access requirements. This leaves a gap in the measure.

The measure would permit public financing for county political party committee races. California county central committee members are elected offices, and the current ban applies broadly to all elective offices. A future program could cover party committee races unless it explicitly excludes them.

The measure permits partial public financing rather than replacing private contributions. Candidates could still accept special interest money up to the spending limits, since most successful programs use matching funds.

Research shows matching systems outperform lump-sum grants at increasing small donor participation. Connecticut and Maine have fuller public financing programs. The spending limit is the key constraint on private money. If limits are set too high, special interest contributions may not be displaced.

The measure prohibits using funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety. General fund money is fungible, so campaign spending could still crowd out other services. The prohibition is a real but incomplete safeguard. The measure does not mandate spending.

Opponents calling the measure a "blank check" is partially true.

The measure authorizes establishing public financing programs through statute, ordinance, resolution, or charter. City council resolutions could potentially create local funds without requiring voter approval or formal ordinances. This raises concerns about weak administrative instruments being used to set program terms.

LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST
SB 42, Umberg.
Political Reform Act of 1974: public campaign financing: California Fair Elections Act of 2026.
Existing law, the Political Reform Act of 1974, prohibits a public officer from expending, and a candidate from accepting, public moneys for the purpose of seeking elective office.
This bill would remove prohibitions imposed on a public officer or candidate to expend or accept public funds, as defined, for the purpose of seeking elective office unless the funds are earmarked by a state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety. The bill would require candidates to abide by specified expenditure limits and meet strict criteria, as defined, to qualify for public funds. The bill would prohibit public funds from being used to pay
legal defense fees or fines or to repay personal loans to their campaign. The bill would permit a statute, ordinance, or charter to establish standards to increase the expenditure limits for each qualified, voluntarily participating candidate pursuant to a specified formula. The bill would provide that the Fair Political Practices Commission is not responsible for administering or enforcing a system of public funding of candidates established by a local governmental agency.
Existing law prohibits a foreign government or foreign principal, as defined, from making a contribution, expenditure, or independent expenditure in connection with the qualification or support of, or opposition to, any state or local ballot measure or in connection with the
election of a candidate to state or local office. Under existing law, a person who violates this prohibition is guilty of a misdemeanor and subject to a fine equal to the amount contributed or expended.
This bill would instead require that a person guilty of
that misdemeanor, in addition to other penalties, be fined an amount at least equal to the amount contributed or expended, but not exceeding a maximum amount of 3 times the amount contributed or expended.
The Political Reform Act of 1974, an initiative measure, provides that the act may be amended by a statute that becomes effective upon approval of the voters.
This bill would require the Secretary of State to submit the provisions of the bill, as specified, to the voters for approval at the November 3, 2026, statewide general
election. This bill would incorporate additional changes to Section 85320 of the Government Code proposed by AB 953 to be operative pursuant to specified conditions.

Bill Text
The people of the State of California do enact as follows:
SECTION 1.
This act shall be known, and may be cited, as the California Fair Elections Act of 2026.
SEC. 2.
The Legislature finds and declares all of the following:
(a) All citizens should be able to make their voices heard in the political process and hold their elected officials accountable.
(b) Elections for local or state elective office should be fair, open, and competitive.
(c) The increasing costs of political campaigns can force candidates to rely on large contributions from wealthy donors and special interests, which can give those wealthy donors and special interests
disproportionate influence over governmental decisions.
(d) Such disproportionate influence can undermine the public’s trust that public officials are performing their duties in an impartial manner and that government is serving the needs and responding to the wishes of all citizens equally, without regard to their wealth.
(e) Special interests contribute more to incumbents than challengers because they seek access to elected officials, and such contributions account for a large portion of the financial incumbency advantage, as confirmed by studies such as those published in the Journal of Politics in 2014 and Political Research Quarterly in 2016.
(f) Citizen-funded election programs, in which qualified candidates can receive
public funds for the purpose of communicating with voters rather than relying exclusively on private donors, are currently operative in five charter cities in California, as well as numerous other local and state jurisdictions.
(g) Citizen-funded election programs encourage competition by reducing the financial advantages of incumbency and making it possible for citizens from all walks of life, not only those with connections to wealthy donors or special interests, to run for office, as confirmed by studies such as those published in State Politics and Policy Quarterly in 2008, and by the Campaign Finance Institute in 2015, the National Institute on Money in State Politics in 2016, and the State Politics and Policy
Quarterly in 2022.
(h) By reducing reliance on wealthy donors and special interests, citizen-funded election programs inhibit improper practices, protect against corruption or the appearance of corruption, and protect the political integrity of our governmental institutions.
(i) In Johnson v. Bradley (1992) 4 Cal.4th 389, the California Supreme Court highlighted the Court of Appeal’s observation that “it seems obvious that public money reduces rather than increases the fund raising pressures on public office seekers and thereby reduces the undue influence of special interest groups.”
(j) In Buckley v. Valeo (1976) 424 U.S. 1, the United States Supreme Court recognized that “public financing as a means of eliminating
the improper influence of large private contributions furthers a significant governmental interest.”
(k) In Arizona Free Enterprise v. Bennett (2011) 564 U.S. 721, the United States Supreme Court acknowledged that public financing of elections “can further ‘significant governmental interest[s]’ such as the state interest in preventing corruption,” quoting Buckley v. Valeo.
(l) In Buckley v. Valeo, the United States Supreme Court further noted that citizen-funded elections programs “facilitate and enlarge public discussion and participation in the electoral process, goals vital to a self-governing people.”
(m) The absolute prohibition on public campaign financing allows special interests to gain disproportionate influence and unfairly
favors incumbents. An exception should be created to permit citizen-funded election programs so that elections may be conducted more fairly.
SEC. 3.
Section 85300 of the Government Code is amended to read:
85300.
(a) A public officer shall not expend, and a candidate shall not accept, any public funds for the purpose of seeking elective office if the funds are earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety.
(b) Candidates shall abide by expenditure limits and meet strict criteria to qualify for public funds.
(c) Public funds shall not be utilized to pay legal defense fees or fines.
(d) (1) A candidate shall not, at any time, use public funds to repay a personal loan to their campaign.
(2) A candidate who receives public funds for their campaign shall not, after their campaign ends, use any source of funds to repay a personal loan to their campaign.
(e) For purposes of this section, the following definitions apply:
(1) “Available candidate funds” means the candidate’s expenditure limit or the sum of all contributions and public funds received by the candidate’s controlled committee for the elective office, whichever is less.
(2) “Expenditure limits” means voluntary spending limits established by statute, ordinance, or charter that qualified, voluntarily participating candidates must abide by to receive public funds.
(3) “Independent expenditures against” means the sum of any expenditures made or expenses incurred by any person or persons for the purpose of making independent expenditures in opposition to a specific candidate.
(4) “Independent expenditures in support” means the sum of any expenditures made or expenses incurred by any person or persons for the purpose of making independent expenditures in support of a specific candidate.
(5) “Net supportive funds” means the sum of available candidate funds,
plus the independent expenditures in support of that candidate, minus the independent expenditures against that candidate.
(6) “Public funds” means any moneys provided to a candidate by a state or local governmental entity for the purpose of seeking elective office.
(7) (A) “Strict criteria” means the requirements set by statute, ordinance, or charter that candidates must meet to receive public funds. (B) (i) If a statute, ordinance, or charter requires a
minimum number of individuals making small-dollar contributions pursuant to subparagraph (A), the largest contribution the statute, ordinance, or charter may require for a contributor to be counted is ten dollars ($10).

I'm weighing the policy merits of Prop 4. The core question is whether to repeal the ban on public campaign funding while preserving its guardrails. I'll examine academic evidence and editorial endorsements before deciding.

The status quo is an outlier. California alone bans public campaign funding, while charter cities already provide it. The ban traces back to Prop 73 in 1988, which also included contribution limits later struck down as unconstitutional. Prop 68 in the same year would have created a public financing program, but Prop 73 won.

The 1988 vote was more nuanced than a simple ban. Prop 68 received 53% of the vote and would have created a public financing system, but Prop 73 won by a larger margin.

Prior rejections targeted specific expensive programs rather than the principle of lifting the ban. Prop 25 in 2000 failed as a broad media voucher system. Prop 89 in 2006 failed as a full clean-money system funded by a corporate tax increase. Prop 15 in 2010 failed as an SOS pilot funded by lobbyist fees.

Prop 4 differs from prior failed measures because it does not mandate a specific statewide program or funding source. Opponents claim voters have rejected taxpayer money for campaigns, but the earlier propositions were not identical. The constitutional landscape also matters: after Buckley and Citizens United, overall spending and independent expenditures cannot be capped.

Contribution limits are already too high and easily circumvented by independent expenditures. Disclosure alone cannot fix the underlying problem. Public financing would give other candidates a floor against self-funded campaigns like Tom Steyer's $213 million spend, though it would not stop such spending entirely.

Empirical evidence from other cities supports public financing. New York's small-donor match produced a broader donor base and more competitive races, enabling candidates of color and women to raise competitively. Seattle's voucher program increased candidate participation by 86% and yielded more representative donors. Connecticut showed more competitive elections and some evidence of reduced corruption convictions.

Other cities show mixed results. Arizona and Maine showed no clear increase in candidates or competitiveness. Oakland's limited program found no reduction in wealthy donor influence. Los Angeles performed worse than New York because of a lower match rate.

The literature confirms that design matters enormously. A well-crafted small-donor matching program can broaden participation and reduce the relative power of large donors.

Prop 4 permits both poorly designed and underfunded programs, which would waste money without meaningful change.

The guardrails are real but incomplete. Candidates must adopt voluntary expenditure limits set by law or charter. They must demonstrate broad-based support through small-dollar contributions or vouchers, not through high per-contributor thresholds, signature counts, or large aggregate fundraising. Earmarked education, transportation, or public safety funds are also prohibited.

Prop 4 also includes anti-abuse provisions. Candidates cannot use public funds for legal defense, fines, or personal loan repayment. This prevents candidates from borrowing money and then raising special-interest funds to repay themselves.

The measure requires nondiscrimination by party or incumbency. It also triples the maximum fine for foreign contributions.

Local choice is a strong argument in favor. The measure does not spend campaign money.

LA Times columnist George Skelton recommended voting yes on this local-control argument.

Supporters include the League of Women Voters, Common Cause, California Clean Money, Consumer Watchdog, nurses, NOW, disability rights groups, the Democratic Party, Newsom, and the Legislature. The Legislature voted 29 to 8 in the Senate and 59 to 20 in the Assembly.

Opposition includes the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, CalTax, and the Family Business Association. The San Francisco Chronicle, San Diego Union-Tribune, and SLO viewpoint also oppose it.

Some former FPPC commissioners, including Dan Schnur and Colleen McAndrews, are among the critics. Their opposition carries more weight than typical taxpayer groups because they are respected reform figures.

The case for voting no is now being examined.

Opponents argue the measure authorizes politicians to design programs that benefit themselves. The FPPC is not responsible for administering or enforcing local systems. There is no requirement for independent ethics commissions. Expenditure limits are set by each jurisdiction and could be meaningless. The "strict criteria" language may be illustrative rather than exhaustive.

The "such as" language in the strict criteria section is illustrative, not exhaustive. The mandatory requirement is simply that candidates demonstrate broad-based support. Subparagraph (C) explicitly bars signature requirements and per-contributor dollar thresholds.

The "strict criteria" requirement is unquantified. A jurisdiction could demand just one small-dollar contribution and still claim broad-based support. That loophole would allow a program to be designed for the benefit of the candidate.

There is also a legal inconsistency in the measure. Expenditure limits must be set by statute, ordinance, or charter. Yet subdivision (g) implies that resolutions can be part of the public funding scheme.

The old law permitted dedicated funds by resolution. The new measure only bars earmarked funds, not general fund appropriations. A council could therefore use a budget resolution to fund a program while still meeting the expenditure limit and criteria requirements.

Prop 4 is vulnerable to future amendments. Subdivisions (e), (f), and (h) can be changed by a two-thirds vote of the Legislature without voter approval. The remaining subdivisions require voter approval.

The vulnerable provisions are the definitions of strict criteria, expenditure limits, and the $10 cap. They also include the formula for raising limits, authorization to increase limits, and FPPC non-responsibility. The core rules—earmark protection, strict criteria requirements, anti-abuse provisions, and nondiscrimination—can only be amended by voters.

The amendment vulnerability is less severe than initially described. Subdivisions (e), (f), and (h) may be changed by a two-thirds Legislature vote under subdivision (a). The word "only" applies to the remaining subdivisions, which require voter approval under subdivision (b).

The amendment vulnerability is moderate rather than fatal. The Legislature could weaken the $10 small-donor threshold or expenditure limits by a two-thirds vote without returning to voters, provided it claims the change furthers the purposes of the Act. Courts may review that claim. The core guardrails are still locked in place.

The core "meet strict criteria" requirement is locked in place, but it relies on the broad definition found in subdivision (e). That definition can still be altered by a two-thirds Legislature vote. This creates a real design weakness.

The measure also fails to limit independent expenditures and special interest money. In the Citizens United era, most campaign funding comes from outside groups rather than direct candidate contributions.

Prop 4 includes a mechanism to raise spending caps when independent expenditures occur. This acknowledges that outside spending can still dominate. Candidates could take public money and max out private contributions, potentially increasing total campaign spending rather than reducing it.

Research shows public financing often fails to lower overall spending or eliminate large donor influence when independent expenditures dominate.

California also faces structural budget problems, which adds fiscal risk.

The LAO estimates the measure could cost hundreds of millions annually. Prop 89 was estimated at roughly $200 million per year. The "as little as $1 per resident" figure is the low end of voluntary local programs, not a cap. General Fund appropriations for schools and healthcare are not protected.

Fungibility undermines the earmark protection. Funds can be moved between programs, so the safeguard is weaker than it appears.

San Francisco's Mark Farrell case shows public financing can be abused when no independent watchdog exists. Prop 4 exempts the FPPC from local enforcement and does not require local ethics commissions. Many California jurisdictions lack strong oversight infrastructure.

The Legislature placed this measure on the ballot itself. Incumbents will design the systems they will use.

Incumbents can still advantage themselves by setting qualification thresholds and match rates that favor candidates with existing donor networks, or by setting them too loosely so fringe candidates drain funds. The people writing the rules are the beneficiaries.

Voters have rejected this concept three times in 2000, 2006, and 2010. They passed a ban in 1988.

A 2016 attempt to pass this measure by the Legislature was rejected by the courts, which ruled that voter approval is required. The burden should be on proponents to offer a specific, well-designed program rather than a permission slip. The San Francisco Chronicle supports public financing in principle but opposes this measure because it lacks best-practice requirements and California has not yet studied its existing charter-city programs.

The foreign money penalty increase is a strategic bundling tactic rather than a reason to vote yes. Recent polling shows strong opposition, with 53 percent of respondents opposing the measure and only 42 percent supporting it.

I generally support public financing as a better constitutional response to money in politics. The current ban is too rigid because it blocks well-designed local experiments outside charter cities. The existing charter-city exemption creates an arbitrary two-tier system based on whether a city has a charter rather than on democratic merit.

The core dilemma is whether to reject an imperfect enabling measure in favor of a better future program, or accept it because the near-permanent ban is the larger problem. The alternative to voting yes is a near-permanent ban.

Specific programs were previously rejected by voters over price and corporate tax concerns. An enabling measure is the only remaining path to get anything on the ballot. If it fails, the ban will likely persist for another decade. Progressive cities and counties outside charter cities are currently blocked from adopting public financing. This measure would let them do so through local charters, ordinances, or voter-initiated measures.

Local voters can design programs too, not just incumbents. The guardrails are imperfect but better than a pure repeal. The 1988 rationale against public financing is weaker today because private spending has exploded since 2010 and the public subsidy would serve as a counterweight rather than the main source.

Reputable organizations such as the League of Women Voters and Common Cause support the measure after reviewing the text. They would not back a permission slip lacking standards.

The Los Angeles Times editorial board also recommends voting yes.

Still, the measure risks becoming a slush fund without hard limits. It asks voters to trust a Legislature that has failed to pass meaningful campaign finance reform despite years of Democratic supermajorities.

The Legislature could have written a specific program into the measure for direct voter approval, but it chose not to. That omission signals an intent to avoid scrutiny of the actual details.

The measure also permits local governments to create public financing programs through ordinary ordinances without holding a local popular vote. This means elected officials—not necessarily local voters—would decide whether to adopt such programs.

The measure creates a new unfunded spending category that state and local officials could tap without constitutional or statutory caps. The general fund is already under pressure, so adding this line item is risky. The uncertain benefits do not clearly outweigh the certain costs, especially if local programs are poorly designed.

The measure only bars candidates from spending funds that are explicitly earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety. All other public financing is permitted as long as candidates meet the strict criteria in sections (b) through (g). Because the FPPC has no enforcement authority over local systems, a candidate who fails to qualify could still receive money and spend it freely.

The FPPC may lack the authority to enforce the PRA against local public financing violations. Section (h) exempts the Commission from local administration, and section (b) is part of the PRA. This creates an enforcement gap.

I will check editorial roundups, LAO analysis, and skeptical academic critiques on whether public financing reduces corruption or gets captured. I am ready to give a confident yes or no.

I will check the Sacramento Bee, Mercury News, and Ballotpedia for additional editorial coverage. I also want to verify whether the measure's trigger mechanism conflicts with Arizona Free Enterprise law. The $10 small-donor threshold only caps the maximum required contribution; local programs could still require smaller amounts.

The $100 cap prevents a small number of wealthy donors from qualifying candidates, but it does not set a minimum or maximum number of donors required. Jurisdictions could demand thousands of small contributions or just a handful of large ones, creating a gaming vector. The measure also appears to lack any requirement that candidates must already be qualified for the ballot.

California also faces structural budget problems, which adds fiscal risk.

The LAO estimates the measure could cost hundreds of millions annually. Prop 89 was estimated at roughly $200 million per year. The "as little as $1 per resident" figure is the low end of voluntary local programs, not a cap. General Fund appropriations for schools and healthcare are not protected.

Fungibility undermines the earmark protection. Funds can be moved between programs, so the safeguard is weaker than it appears.

San Francisco's Mark Farrell case shows public financing can be abused when no independent watchdog exists. Prop 4 exempts the FPPC from local enforcement and does not require local ethics commissions. Many California jurisdictions lack strong oversight infrastructure.

The Legislature placed this measure on the ballot itself. Incumbents will design the systems they will use.

Incumbents can still advantage themselves by setting qualification thresholds and match rates that favor candidates with existing donor networks, or by setting them too loosely so fringe candidates drain funds. The people writing the rules are the beneficiaries.

Voters have rejected this concept three times in 2000, 2006, and 2010. They passed a ban in 1988.

A 2016 attempt to pass this measure by the Legislature was rejected by the courts, which ruled that voter approval is required. The burden should be on proponents to offer a specific, well-designed program rather than a permission slip. The San Francisco Chronicle supports public financing in principle but opposes this measure because it lacks best-practice requirements and California has not yet studied its existing charter-city programs.

The foreign money penalty increase is a strategic bundling tactic rather than a reason to vote yes. Recent polling shows strong opposition, with 53 percent of respondents opposing the measure and only 42 percent supporting it.

I generally support public financing as a better constitutional response to money in politics. The current ban is too rigid because it blocks well-designed local experiments outside charter cities. The existing charter-city exemption creates an arbitrary two-tier system based on whether a city has a charter rather than on democratic merit.

The core dilemma is whether to reject an imperfect enabling measure in favor of a better future program, or accept it because the near-permanent ban is the larger problem. The alternative to voting yes is a near-permanent ban.

Specific programs were previously rejected by voters over price and corporate tax concerns. An enabling measure is the only remaining path to get anything on the ballot. If it fails, the ban will likely persist for another decade. Progressive cities and counties outside charter cities are currently blocked from adopting public financing. This measure would let them do so through local charters, ordinances, or voter-initiated measures.

Local voters can design programs too, not just incumbents. The guardrails are imperfect but better than a pure repeal. The 1988 rationale against public financing is weaker today because private spending has exploded since 2010 and the public subsidy would serve as a counterweight rather than the main source.

Reputable organizations such as the League of Women Voters and Common Cause support the measure after reviewing the text. They would not back a permission slip lacking standards.

The Los Angeles Times editorial board also recommends voting yes.

Still, the measure risks becoming a slush fund without hard limits. It asks voters to trust a Legislature that has failed to pass meaningful campaign finance reform despite years of Democratic supermajorities.

The Legislature could have written a specific program into the measure for direct voter approval, but it chose not to. That omission signals an intent to avoid scrutiny of the actual details.

The measure also permits local governments to create public financing programs through ordinary ordinances without holding a local popular vote. This means elected officials—not necessarily local voters—would decide whether to adopt such programs.

The measure creates a new unfunded spending category that state and local officials could tap without constitutional or statutory caps. The general fund is already under pressure, so adding this line item is risky. The uncertain benefits do not clearly outweigh the certain costs, especially if local programs are poorly designed.

The measure only bars candidates from spending funds that are explicitly earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety. All other public financing is permitted as long as candidates meet the strict criteria in sections (b) through (g). Because the FPPC has no enforcement authority over local systems, a candidate who fails to qualify could still receive money and spend it freely.

The FPPC may lack the authority to enforce the PRA against local public financing violations. Section (h) exempts the Commission from local administration, and section (b) is part of the PRA. This creates an enforcement gap.

I will check editorial roundups, LAO analysis, and skeptical academic critiques on whether public financing reduces corruption or gets captured. I am ready to give a confident yes or no.

I will check the Sacramento Bee, Mercury News, and Ballotpedia for additional editorial coverage. I also want to verify whether the measure's trigger mechanism conflicts with Arizona Free Enterprise law. The $10 small-donor threshold only caps the maximum required contribution; local programs could still require smaller amounts.

The $100 cap prevents a small number of wealthy donors from qualifying candidates, but it does not set a minimum or maximum number of donors required. Jurisdictions could demand thousands of small contributions or just a handful of large ones, creating a gaming vector. # The Telescoping Effects of Public Campaign Funding: Evaluating the Impact of Clean Elections in Arizona, Maine, and New Jersey
### Abstract
Supporters of public campaign funding say it democratizes the election process; detractors say it fails to meet its intended goals and, in fact, has unexpected negative results.
Examining data from Arizona and Maine, which have full public funding, and from New Jersey's “Clean Election” pilot program, has enabled us to determine empirically if critics are correct.
We conclude that neither advocates of Clean Elections nor its detractors are completely accurate.
Rather, public campaign funding enhances trends that already existed where it was implemented without sparking new ones.

The Political Reform Act. Many people, groups, and businesses spend money to support or
oppose candidates for public office and ballot measures. California’s Political Reform Act sets
rules for how money can be used in politics and requires public reporting of political spending.
These rules apply to state and local candidates, ballot measures, and other public officials, but
not to federal candidates or officials. (Federal law establishes campaign finance and reporting
requirements for federal offices.) The Political Reform Act has been updated by voters over the
years.
Ban on Public Funds to Pay for Campaigns. The Political Reform Act bans the use of
public funds for political candidates’ campaigns. This ban applies to most elected offices at the
state level and local level. (This ban does not apply to city office elections in certain charter
cities. Los Angeles, San Francisco, Long Beach, Oakland, and Berkeley are current examples of
charter cities that provide public funds to certain campaigns.)
Entities That Oversee Campaign Finance Laws. California’s campaign finance laws are
administered by the Fair Political Practices Commission and the California Secretary of State.
State law requires people and groups to report how much money they give, receive, and spend on
political campaigns. This information is available to the public on the Secretary of State’s
website. The Fair Political Practices Commission enforces and interprets the Political Reform
Act. The Fair Political Practices Commission reviews the finance reports and can fine candidates
and donors who break the law. The Fair Political Practices Commission issues guidance based on
its interpretation of the Political Reform Act.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 2 of 3
PROPOSAL
Lifts Ban on Use of Public Funds to Pay for Candidates’ Campaigns. Proposition 4 lifts the
ban on using public funds for political candidates’ campaigns. Removing the ban allows state
and local governments to create public campaign financing programs in the future if they wish.
Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance system for the state or local
governments directly.
Sets Rules for Future State and Local Public Campaign Finance Programs. Proposition 4
sets broad rules for future state and local public campaign finance programs but leaves many key
design decisions to future state and local decision makers. Proposition 4 limits which public
funds can be used for campaigns, who can receive the funds, and how the funds can be spent in
any future public campaign finance program. For example, money meant for education,
transportation, or public safety cannot be used for campaigns. Candidates can only receive public
funds if they show broad-based support in their district and agree to spending limits and other
program rules. Public funds cannot be used for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a
candidate’s personal campaign loan. State and local governments can design and implement their
own programs within the broad rules set by Proposition 4.
Fair Political Practices Commission Would Issue Guidance on Public Campaign Finance
Programs. Proposition 4 specifies that the Fair Political Practices Commission is not required to
administer or enforce local public campaign finance programs. Rather, state and local
government officials could ask the Fair Political Practices Commission for guidance on how to
create public campaign finance programs consistent with Proposition 4.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Costs of Possible Public Campaign Finance Programs Depend on Future Decisions.
Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance program. However, it allows state and
local governments to create such programs in the future. The cost of these programs could be
significant for governments that choose to create them. The total cost would depend on which
governments created such programs and how those programs were designed.
Minor State Costs to Support State and Local Governments Considering Public Campaign
Finance Programs. If voters approve Proposition 4, state and local government officials likely
would ask the Fair Political Practices Commission for guidance on creating public campaign
finance programs under the Political Reform Act. This likely would require the Fair Political
Practices Commission to hire more legal staff to help answer these questions. As a result, state
costs would be a few hundred thousand dollars each year. This amount is much less than one-
tenth of 1 percent (0.1 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the
account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and
prisons.)
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 3 of 3
YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: State and local governments could create public
campaign financing programs for public office candidates, subject to limits on which public
funds could be used, how the public funds could be used, and who could receive them.
A NO vote on this measure means: State and most local governments would remain unable to
create public campaign finance programs for public office candidates.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair
Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments
about public campaign finance programs.
BALLOT LABEL
Fiscal Impact: Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the
Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about
public campaign finance programs.

Checking McClatchy's yes and Mercury News' no reasoning more carefully. Also looking for full editorials from the Sacramento Bee or LA Times.

Enough information gathered. The vote removes a legal ban and sets minimum conditions without spending money on campaigns. Future programs would require separate political decisions.

The strongest argument against the measure is that it creates an incomplete permission structure. It allows officials to create programs by ordinance without another public vote. It lacks independent enforcement and meaningful caps on subsidies. Public money could stack on special-interest money. Several editorial boards that agree with the underlying concern still oppose it.

The strongest argument for yes is that the ban itself is the binding constraint blocking good programs. Charter cities already experiment with these laws, but the ban arbitrarily prevents everyone else from doing so. Specific statewide programs failed at the ballot because they included tax increases and one-size-fits-all designs. An opt-in enabling law is the correct institutional response to that history.

The measure includes stronger guardrails than opponents claim. It bans loan repayments and legal defense spending. It sets a $10 small-dollar limit. It protects against earmarks. It mandates spending limits and nondiscrimination.

Voluntary public financing is one of the few constitutional tools left in a post-Citizens United world.

The League of Women Voters, Common Cause, and Clean Money Campaign support it. McClatchy and the LA Times Skelton also say yes.

A no vote preserves a system where only personal wealth and large donors fund campaigns. That is worse than the risk of some poorly designed local programs.

The recommendation is yes. A failed vote would leave the statewide ban intact, and poorly designed programs could not be repealed locally. Charter cities are already exempt from that ban.

About 125 of California's 482 cities are charter cities. Most local governments are general law and remain banned. Counties are also prohibited from using public funds for campaigns.

The LAO and AG summaries disagree on whether charter counties are exempt from the ban. The LAO cites only certain charter cities, while the AG summary includes counties. The Johnson v. Bradley ruling applies home rule protections to charter cities but not to counties.

If only charter cities are exempt, counties would remain banned. County offices and state offices receive heavy special interest funding. This is a major concern. I will verify whether charter counties are also exempt.

I am also checking whether the measure's trigger mechanism is constitutional. I will verify whether its flaws are fatal enough to warrant a rejection. My leaning remains yes. The expected value of passing is moderate: several cities and possibly the state would experiment with well-designed small-donor match programs.

Clean Money and Common Cause would push for sound designs, and existing programs would serve as models. Some cities might still create weak or captured programs. Nondiscrimination rules and spending limits would constrain the worst abuses. Bad programs could be defunded by future budgets because they are not constitutional entitlements.

The measure does not appropriate a fixed sum. A bad program is reversible by the same body that created it, or by voters via referendum or initiative.

Passing would let more non-wealthy candidates run, strengthen small-donor power, and allow voluntary spending limits that are otherwise unconstitutional to impose. It would also reduce dependence on large donors in participating races.

A no vote preserves the status quo where billionaire self-funders and independent expenditure committees dominate. Qualified non-wealthy candidates stay out of races. Charter cities keep their programs, but everyone else remains blocked from experimentation.

The "wait for a better measure" strategy has failed for 38 years. A no vote is not a vote for reform; it is a vote to preserve the ban. The measure locks in permission rather than spending, so wasteful programs can be ended without another statewide constitutional fight.

The option value of lifting the ban outweighs keeping it. Bad programs can be ended locally, while good ones are currently impossible outside charter cities.

The Chronicle's call to study first is weak. Existing charter city programs have been available for decades without study. Waiting for a study that nobody is commissioning is a reason to delay forever. Studying those programs does not require maintaining the ban on new ones.

The blank check argument is overstated. A yes vote only authorizes future appropriations that would still go through normal budget processes, and existing local programs are modest. The lack of independent enforcement remains the strongest anti-argument, but it is not decisive.

The PRA's disclosure rules still apply to public campaign funds. The FPPC retains enforcement authority over contribution limits and prohibitions in 85300(a)-(d) and (g)-(h). It only excuses itself from administering local public financing systems. A candidate who uses public funds for legal defense would violate the PRA. Local prosecutors, civil litigants, and local ethics bodies can enforce that prohibition.

Opposition claims that the measure lacks spending limits, strict criteria, or that it would drain school and public safety funds are incorrect. The text explicitly requires expenditure limits and defines the $10 small-donor threshold. Earmarked funds are prohibited, and any general fund tradeoffs would be a local choice rather than a mandate.

Opposition claims that thousands of candidates will automatically receive money are incorrect; the measure only authorizes future programs and requires local qualification. The argument that it allows special interest money is misleading because the current system already permits such funding, and matching systems are designed to work alongside limited private contributions.

Supporter overclaims should be rejected. The claim that elections will be "won not bought" is overstated because independent expenditure committees and self-funding remain possible. The "$1 per resident" figure is marketing hyperbole rather than a binding cap.

The URL points to the 2026 public financing measure, not a 2024 climate bond. The recommendation remains yes.

I considered a steelman argument for no: public financing only works if private money is replaced by tightly capped public funds with strong enforcement, and Prop 4 does not lock that in. I rejected it. The recommendation remains yes.

The measure authorizes additive public subsidies with caps and qualification rules written by beneficiaries, enforced by nobody in particular. Empirical evidence shows that poorly designed programs do not reduce donor influence. California's track record of interest-group capture makes this especially risky. The Legislature had the opportunity to propose a specific, capped, independently administered program, but chose a blank permission structure instead because voters reject specific programs.

The measure is not a true laboratory of democracy. It avoids voter accountability for program costs. Voters have rejected similar proposals three times. The foreign-money penalty is a Trojan sweetener. Former FPPC chairs oppose the measure. Multiple editorial boards, including the Chronicle, also oppose it.

The no vote is fiscally responsible and institutionally careful. A better measure would require independent administration, minimum small-donor thresholds, capped public subsidies, and mandatory rejection of large contributions. The choice is between Prop 4 and the ban, not between this measure and a hypothetical ideal.

The ideal program is not on the ballot and is unlikely to appear, given prior rejections. A no vote would kill reform by demanding perfection. The measure is a floor, not a ceiling. Implementing statutes and ordinances can add strong safeguards after passage. Cities can still adopt well-designed local systems.

The Chronicle's call for both maximum local freedom and mandated best practices is internally inconsistent. Lange's approach of maximum freedom is consistent with the measure's theory.

The risk that jurisdictions will choose bad designs is mitigated by annual budget visibility, reversibility, and existing models to copy.

The recommendation remains yes.

The SF Chronicle, the most sophisticated local policy voice, voted no. That carries significant weight.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)

The influence of money on political races has gotten out of control, but allowing candidates to accept public funds — taxpayer dollars — for campaign purposes is not the answer.
We recommend voting “no” on Proposition 4. Our tax dollars should not be spent on election campaigns.

Endorsement: Reject San Mateo Community College District’s $848 million Measure V (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-reject-san-mateo-community-college-districts-848-million-measure-v/)

Sky-high spending
Consider this news organization’s report last week (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/11/whos-donating-to-the-billionaire-backed-group-has-raised-almost-300-million-to-fight-the-wealth-tax/) showing how a single political action committee backed by billionaires — Building a Better California — has spent nearly a quarter of a billion dollars this year alone, breaking all previous records.
Understandably alarmed, this inundation of money into state politics has pushed legislators to ask voters this November to repeal a 1988 law and allow taxpayer dollars to be spent on campaigns.
A “yes” vote would allow state and local governments to create programs so that public funds — again, taxpayer dollars — could be set aside for election campaigns.
We understand the desire to take corporate money out of elections.
This year’s race for California governor (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/california-governor-contributions-takeaways/) highlights that need more than ever. A political spending committee comprising the state realtors association, California Chamber of Commerce, Pacific Gas & Electric and the state electrical workers union spent a record $32 million on ads opposing Democratic billionaire Tom Steyer, who ultimately placed third in the primary.
Leading into those primaries, Democratic nominee Xavier Becerra — whose name appears on the Nov. 3 ballot — was backed by Meta, AirBnB and Uber at $1 million each and Chevron, McDonalds and DaVita at $500,000 each, to name a few.
Those corporate dollars force the fair question: If elected, how confident are we that Becerra will have the people’s interests at heart, and not those corporations’?
Not solution
Many counties are already struggling financially. Some have placed sales tax measures on the ballot this year to bring more revenue into their general funds. Some already had sales tax measures on the ballot in 2024. And some still face a budget deficit. Other counties may be sitting on the fence, but there is no wiggle room in their budgets to create a fund for campaign financing.
Moreover, people should be able to decide if they want their money to go toward supporting a candidate. Our elected officials should not make that decision for us — especially if they are up for re-election.
We agree that special interests should not be able to buy candidates or campaigns, but Proposition 4 is not the answer. Creating a fund of taxpayer dollars and making it available for election campaigns is not the answer. Those hard-earned dollars belong in a municipality’s general fund, to be used on improving roadways, funding for public safety officers or enhancing our local parks.
Reject Proposition 4.

McClatchy Media’s endorsements for all 14 propositions on California’s ballot
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
Updated October 27, 2026 9:16 AM
The California state Capitol on Aug. 31, 2026.
Lauren Chapman
lchapman@sacbee.com
Opinion journalists for McClatchy Media conducted interviews with supporters and opponents of all 14 statewide propositions on your November ballot. The journalists then deliberated and decided how they would vote on each one, just as voters do. Their endorsements, linked below, explain their positions.
What to Know
Here are key takeaways:
Prop. 1 would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds for affordable housing and CalVet home loans (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317326136.html#storylink=var-wtk), with $10 billion aimed at closing financing gaps for nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes already in the pipeline. The board endorsed a “yes” vote but urged the state to publish a transparent dashboard tracking costs and results.
Prop. 2 would raise California’s rainy day fund cap from 10% to 20% (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317091637.html#storylink=var-wtk) of annual tax collections and allow some reserves to pay down state debts, including $20 billion still owed to the federal government for pandemic-era unemployment borrowing. The board recommended a “yes” vote as a safeguard against future downturns.
Prop. 3 would make permanent a tax on California’s top 2% of earners (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317445836.html#storylink=var-wtk) — single filers making at least $361,000 and joint filers at least $721,000 — that generates between $5 billion and $15 billion a year for schools and community colleges. The board endorsed a “yes” vote.
Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on public financing of state and local campaigns (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317448027.html#storylink=var-wtk), allowing matching-fund or public-grant programs for qualifying candidates. The board backed a “yes” vote, arguing public financing reduces reliance on wealthy donors.
Prop. 5 would eliminate the second question on recall ballots asking who should replace an ousted official (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316911387.html#storylink=var-wtk), instead triggering special elections or gubernatorial appointments. The board strongly endorsed a “yes” vote, noting past recalls have installed replacements with less voter support than the official removed.
Prop. 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to finance second mortgages (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317470188.html#storylink=var-wtk) covering up to 17% of a new home’s price for middle-class buyers. Despite reservations about default risk, the board recommended a “yes” vote.
Prop. 38 proposes an $8.4 billion bond for immunology research (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166634.html#storylink=var-wtk), with half guaranteed to an institute tied to UCLA and backed by billionaire physician Gary K. Michelson. The board urged a “no” vote, warning the measure would exempt the institute from public-records laws.
Prop. 39 would require government-issued ID at the polls and partial ID numbers on mail ballots (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317017898.html#storylink=var-wtk), with backers including nine billionaires tracked by Forbes. The board recommended a “no” vote, warning the measure would disenfranchise more legitimate voters than it would stop fraudulent ones.
Prop. 40 would impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on Californians worth more than $1 billion (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317269166.html#storylink=var-wtk), with 90% of proceeds reserved for healthcare amid federal Medi-Cal cuts projected to cost 1.3 million residents coverage by 2030. A majority of the board endorsed a “yes” vote.
Prop. 41 is a constitutional amendment backed by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other wealthy donors that would ban taxes exempt from state spending limits on or after Jan. 1, 2026 (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html#storylink=var-wtk) — a provision that could nullify Prop. 40. The board urged a “no” vote.
Prop. 42 is billed as a safeguard for 401(k) accounts and personal property, but the board called it a “poison pill” designed to derail the billionaire wealth tax (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166989.html#storylink=var-wtk) in Prop. 40. If Prop. 42 gets more yes votes than Prop. 40, Prop. 40 would not take effect. Vote “no,” the board said.
Prop. 43 would raise the threshold to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives from a simple majority to 66.7% (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316956235.html#storylink=var-wtk), giving a 33.3% minority the power to block measures funding fire, police, flood control and other local services. The board opposed it and urged a “no” vote.
Prop. 44, the Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act, would require federally qualified health centers to spend at least 90% of revenue on patient services (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317472706.html#storylink=var-wtk), up from the roughly 80% most currently report. The board recommended a “no” vote, citing warnings the mandate could force clinics serving nearly 7 million patients to close.
Prop. 45 would reshape the California Environmental Quality Act (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317475362.html#storylink=var-wtk) by tightening deadlines, limiting public-comment periods and barring judges from halting entire projects over partial violations. The board endorsed a “yes” vote, arguing CEQA has too often been used to block needed housing.
The summary points above were compiled with the help of AI tools and edited by journalists. The source reporting referenced above was written and edited entirely by journalists.

I have enough information to decide.

I will vote yes. The measure is an enabling statute, not an appropriation. The current ban arbitrarily blocks most counties and cities from exploring public financing. Only about 121 charter cities are allowed to experiment with it.

The 1988 ban specifically blocked Sacramento County's local experiment. Empirical evidence supports small-donor matching and vouchers, models already used in California cities. Prop 4's criteria align with these existing approaches.

Prop 4 steers toward small-donor matching and vouchers rather than unlimited grants. It requires broad-based support and spending limits. Opponents' claims are overstated. The measure does not provide blank checks. It protects earmarked funds and bans using public money for legal defense or personal loans.

The measure has implementation weaknesses. It lacks an independent enforcement mandate and a numeric floor for broad-based support. Caps are set later, and local programs may coexist with private money. The FPPC is not required to enforce local programs. Definitional sections can be amended by two-thirds vote.

These are watchful implementation concerns rather than reasons to keep the blanket ban. Implementing laws can add protections. Bad programs are budget decisions that can be reversed. The current ban cannot be reversed locally.

Prior rejections targeted specific costly statewide programs with dedicated taxes, not local options. The Legislature explicitly notes this distinction.

Good-government organizations with subject-matter expertise support the measure. Taxpayer associations oppose it on principle against any public campaign spending.
